subtopic: DENIAL OF ALLEGATION CONCERNING STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO INSPECTOR DAWSON
speechtext: Yesterday the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) made an inquiry of me in regard to a return which I had submitted a few days ago respecting certain reports of Inspector Dawson of the penitentiary branch. The hon. member stated that while the return went up to April 8, 1934, on April 9 Inspector Dawson had an inte"'-view with prisoner 3033 in the penitentiary. I have made a pretty full inquiry in regard to this matter since yesterday, and I find that Inspector Dawson went to the penitentiary to make an inspection and report respecting a certain matter which had been referred to him. After he had concluded his inspection on April 8, an interview was requested by prisoner 3033 and it is during the course of that interview I think it is alleged by the hon. member for Southeast Grey that certain aspersions were made against her character as stated by her yesterday. I can assure her that there is no foundation for the report. The inspector himself made no report on this interview. When inspectors or superintendents visit a penitentiary, they have a large number of requests for interviews, but they do not make specific reports in regard to them. However Inspector Dawson has assured me most definitely that during his interview with prisoner 3033 the name of the hon. member for Southeast Grey was never mentioned by him or by the prisoner, there was no comment whatever in regard to her, and I can assure her on the word of honour of the inspector that there is no foundation for the allegation which she has made.

speechtext: Has the government received any representations from the bondholders of the Grand Trunk Railway in London or from a representative thereof, protesting that they should have been consulted, under their statutory rights, as outlined in section 31, Grand Trunk Act, 1862, and Grand Trunk Act, 1873, to vote for or agree to auditors, and further protesting against the passing of Bill No. 20, as passed by the House of Commons on March 5, 1935, until they were so consulted and had an opportunity to express their wishes regarding the appointment of auditors?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: PROTEST OF GRAND TRUNK SHAREHOLDERS AGAINST APPOINTMENT OF AUDITORS WITHOUT CONSULTATION
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was
courteous enough to advise me this morning that he was going t.o ask this question, so I looked into the matter thoroughly in order to have a proper reply, because of the importance of the subject. Because of that importance I intend to read my reply, in order to avoid any possible misunderstanding, as it may perhaps be transmitted to London.
Two communications have been received, not from bondholders, as stated by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), but from former preference shareholders whose stocks were . declared of no value by the Grand Trunk board of arbitration, 1921. One was received by the hon. the Speaker, and the other by the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris), as chairman of the railway committee of the house. Each made representations in the terms referred to by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough.
The correspondents were informed that the appointment of auditors of Canadian National Railways had nothing whatever to do with any controversy concerning the alleged rights of former Grand Trunk stockholders, the auditors being appointed by parliament each year, as required by the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act of 1933. They are not company auditors, but auditors for parliament.
As to the voting rights of former shareholders, attention was directed to the fact that section 4 of the Grand Trunk Acquisition Act of 1919 reads as follows:
Provided that concurrently with such guarantee of dividends and interest upon the present guaranteed stock and the present debenture

stocks, respectively, the voting powers at meetings of shareholders of the Grand Trunk now vested in or exercisable by the holders of the said stocks respectively shall cease and determine absolutely.
This proviso was also incorporated in the formal agreement between the London Grand Trunk management and the Canadian government.

speechtext:
Just one word, Mr. Chairman, and I will be through. Some time ago from the Montreal Star I quoted an excerpt from a speech by the right hon. Prime Minister with regard to the newsprint industry and the blank cheque legislation. I believe I am in order now in referring to that matter again. The quotation was as follows:
Mr. Bennett, with a chuckle, told the audience that he had had one satisfaction the other day, when representatives of the pulp and paper industry of Canada had come and asked him whether if the provinces of Quebec and Ontario request that the government do so they would make effective one of their laws which the Liberals opposed-he had the satisfaction of their asking the government to do that which Mr. King asked his followers to vote against- "and I listened while Mr. Taschereau and Mr. Hepburn asked us to make it effective in their interest-those are some of the compensations of public life, remarked the premier.
Here I have a letter from a very distinguished gentleman, a noble son of the good old province of Ontario, the Hon. Mitchell F. Hepburn, dated Toronto, Februay 28, 1935. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Pouliot:
In reply to your letter of February 26th, I desire to make it very clear that the only correspondence I had with Prime Minister Bennett was contained in a telegram dated November 7th, which telegram was sent following representations of members of the newsprint industry who desired a conference with federal authorities. You will note that I stated that details of application of any federal policy would be open to consideration and approval by the Ontario government. No mention was made of applying the blank cheque legislation as contained in the peace, order and good government act, which I oppose in prinfMr. McIntosh.]
ciple, nor, as far as I can ascertain, in the industry itself in favour of application of provisions of this act.	.
You will therefore note that the extract from the speech of Mr. Bennett appearing in the Montreal Star, which reads:
The quotation I have read follows, and the letter continues:
... if correctly reported, indicates clearly that he did go beyond the construction I intended to put upon the contents of the telegram itself. You will further note that no representative of the Ontario government appeared at the conference in response to the invitation extended by Prime Minister Bennett.
With kind personal regards, I am,
Sincerely yours,
M. F. Hepburn.
Jean-Franqois Pouliot, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
That is the first part of it. Now, sir, let me read the telegram which was sent by Mr. Hepburn to the right hon. Prime Minister and which was tabled by the Secretary of State on February 15, 1935, in sessional paper No. 160:
1934, November 7. Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, Iv.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
I believe situation of newsprint industry now makes it advisable for manufacturers to discuss problem writh you.
The Ontario government will support a policy of federal action to remedy the industry with details of application open to consideration and approval.
And that is signed by M. F. .Hepburn. This is not complete, because Mr. Taschereau was mentioned by the right hon. gentleman as well as Mr. Hepburn. I have before me a flat denial given by Mr. Taschereau along the same lines as the one given by Mr. Hepburn. It reads as follows:
(Translation):
Province of Quebec Office of the Premier
Quebec, March 16, 1935. Mr. J. F. Pouliot, K.C., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Pouliot:
I have your letter of the 12th instant, to which I hasten to reply.
As the file produced by Hon. Mr. Bennett show's, I neither wwote nor telegraphed to him regarding his interview w'ith the paper manufacturers. I have never, in any manner whatsoever, either directly or indirectly, approved the blank cheque given him by the House of Commons.
You are not unaware of the fact that I have been in very active touch with the paper manufacturers in an effort to find a solution to the problem existing to-day, particularly in Ontario

Economic Council
and Quebec, and to remedy a situation that threatens to become disastrous to the paper industry.
In the course of an interview at Quebec with some of the manufacturers, it was suggested that Mr. Bennett be asked to prevent the export of paper to the United States unless it was sold at a certain price which would be sufficiently remunerative to the industry. I was asked to telephone to Mr. Bennett, at Ottawa, to ask him if he would receive a delegation. I did so immediately, and Mr. Bennett told me he would receive the delegation at a date which has now escaped my mind.
_ I understand that the representatives of the industry did go to Ottawa. I took no part in the interview the delegation had with the Prime Minister of Canada.
I think the above sufficiently answers your inquiry.
Sincerely yours,
L. A. Taschereau.
Therefore the assumption by the right hon. Prime Minister that he had the support of the premiers of Ontario and Quebec was all wrong. I shall not say much about it, but I am complaining about the condition Of the lumberjacks in the province of Quebec and the conditions of all those people who have suffered since' the blank cheque legislation was passed. I shall have more to say later, but shall simply place these letters on record at the present time.

I would object to anyone but you, Mr. Chairman, being appointed chairman of this council.
We have no information about that. The right hon. acting Prime Minister states, "Well, it will not cost much; it will not cost much." They say the radio commission was not to cost much, but it costs a million dollars each year. They say it effects great economy, but it is only a disturbance to the listeners over the radio. speechtext:
Here I object to it. If the Prime Minister is chairman of the council he cannot support himself. I say this is a most absurd proposition. Here we have a council set up to assist the Prime Minister, and yet we find that the Prime Minister is chairman of that council. So far as I am concerned that seems to be the most foolish thing on earth. We have the Prime Minister supporting himself. He will be the legs and the head of the council. The acting Prime Minister must know about this, and I must say I am strongly apposed to it. The bill provides crutches for a moribund government. If the government has no information, then the only thing it could do would be to attend a correspondence school or subscribe to the Columbia lectures, and in that way get some information about economics. When we ask them questions we find that sometimes they are like fence posts; no answers come from their mouths. I know they are not children. Truth comes from the mouths of babes, but from the mouths of the ministers comes no information. Why? It is because they do not wish to have any information and because they are kept up by patronage and other silly things, rather than giving their time to the business of the state. Every person must strongly object because people find this condition most ridiculous. We have a flood of boards; in fact it would seem that we are to have a soviet government in Canada, a government by irresponsible men who will dictate the policies.
Yesterday we heard a great, deal about statistics. I wonder if the acting Prime Minister knows how those statistics are compiled. He may receive information from the bureau of statistics and then do his own thinking upon them. Then, if the Prime Minister cannot act the chairman would be, ex officio
Economic Council

the acting Prime Minister. I wonder how he could do his work without the assistance of that council. I am sorry to have to make these observations because I realize he is older than I am, but I know any member other than a cabinet minister could dispense with the council. When they ask for a steak is it necessary to have someone cut their meat, in order that they may have a mouthful which would not choke them? They are just like children; they do not know how to work, and they must have some people to cut their meat, just as children would have. What a spectacle before the country! Here we have a government, it has been said, of supermen, men far above the average. But they cannot do anything for themselves. They have to be run about in the wheel chair of bureaucracy. They need a tutor and a guardian. Tutors and guardians are only appointed for children who are not of age and for those who cannot attend to their own business. But here we have a government of supermen, semi-gods, and they are asking for relief; they complain that they have too much work to do. I sincerely hope from the bottom of my heart that the acting Prime Minister and his colleagues, some of whom are able men, will not insist on this measure. They know that it is absurd. We have had enough of this stuff. We have had enough of those people who try to put false ideas in the heads of the ministers who form the government of this country. Who will take this government seriously when they submit such a bill as this to the house? I am sorry for the acting Prime Minister. I know that he does not need my sympathy because he is an able man, a superman, and therefore needs it -much less than others, but why should such a burden be imposed on him?

speechtext: I say that the hon. gentleman assumes that I shall continue acting as Prime Minister. There is no ground for that assumption whatever. After this bill is passed and this council is set up there may be some other gentleman who will act in the absence of the Prime Minister of the day.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION OP BODY TO COORDINATE WORK OF DEPARTMENTS AND TO INVESTIGATE AND ADVISE UPON SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
On that point I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman because there will ibe a turn of the tide at the next election, but just now I take this view. At present the right hon. gentleman is acting Prime Minister. He is so either in virtue- of an order in council which has been passed recently or in virtue of an order in council which was passed some time ago providing that whenever the Prime Minister was unable to attend to his duties he would be replaced ipso facto by the right hon. gentleman. Therefore the right hon. gentleman is the acting Prime Minister. That is my humble opinion and I am sure he will not deny it. Therefore if he is acting Prime Minister so long as this government is in power, I do not see how another vice chairman of the board could be appointed because if this legislation is necessary, if it is necessary for the government to have such an economic council, and if the Prime Minister is to be chairman of that board, the acting Prime Minister will be superseded by the vice chair-

Economic Council
man, which is absurd. It will mean that the acting head of the government will play second fiddle on the council, and that is why I object.
I think that those who have drafted this bill have been most inconsiderate of the acting Prime Minister. Precisely,
an echo. We have had an illustration of this in the great country to the south where a brain trust has been operated and directed by just the type of mentality as one would anticipate will be directing this council. I think this will be the case whether the Conservative party is to have the direction of it or whether my friends to the right happen to come into power. A very frank report has recently been made upon the operations of the National Industrial Recovery Act. This report was prepared by the research and political division of the NRA and, therefore, has the imprimatur of authority upon it. The meat of the report is contained in seven lines, totalling ninety-five words, which appear on page 24 of the report. These seven lines sum up boldly and devastatingly the effect of the NRA and the results of the actions of the brain trust in that country. I quote:

Note that although payrolls in December, 1934, were only about 60 per cent of the total in 1926, dividends and interest were 150 per cent of their total in 1926. In short, the income enjoyed by those who received dividends and interest was 50 per cent'higher than in 1926, even though the national income has declined' nearly 40 per cent since that date and volume of production has declined by one-third ... clearly the recipients of profits have not failed to enjoy their proportionate share of the increase in industrial recovery.
That is taken from the official report of the operations of the NRA. It is very clear that in spite of the ballyhooing which has taken place in the press and the radio speeches which have been delivered, the NRA, directed as it is by a capitalistic minded government, has been directed with the idea of sustaining the profits of the few to the extent which they could be sustained and of passing on as little as possible to the masses. That that has been the result is proven by this report. I therefore suggest this thought to the committee, that any such economic council as is now being proposed under the guidance and direction of those who would continue the existing system, can mean in the long run just precisely the result that has already been shown in the United States in its attempt to do the very same thing with the system.
I could go further afield as I have done on another occasion and produce similar illustrations of the futility of attempting to regulate or direct capitalism by any economic council of any kind whatever. In short, the fruitfulness or usefulness of an economic council will depend entirely upon the policy behind its creation, the policy for which it is established. I contend with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin that the primary policy that should be the very basis of every activity of this economic council should be to ascertain first the potential productivity of the country, something concerning which we have no accurate information; to correlate those facts; to ascertain the total consumption of which the country is capable if real demand were satisfied, and to bring those two functions into harmony so as to make it possible for the Canadian people to consume the maximum quantity of what they produce. If that be the purpose of the council, then indeed it may be fruitful, it may justify the not overly enthusiastic praise of the hon. member for Red Deer yesterday when he said that he was glad to see that the proposal made by him on behalf of this section of the house was at last bearing fruit. As I heard him say that," it occurred to me that he was in the position of a gentleman who had planted a McIntosh Red and was now reaching out his hand to collect a very

Economic Council
sour and very small crabapple. That is just about what this economic council appears to be in the light of the suggestion made from this corner. We never envisioned such a thing as a prime minister's committee; we want a national council that will undertake to discover in an effective way the productive powers of the country and then advise as to how best the maximum consumption by the people of Canada may take place.
While I am on my feet, may I suggest that the idea of having this council tied up to the Prime Minister and his department shows a great weakness. This council should have complete freedom of action without direction or interference from any authority other than that which is laid down as a matter of definite policy to be pursued, a definite objective to be obtained, such as the one which has been already outlined by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. To tie up such a committee for example to the national research council would also be a mistake. May I pause here just momentarily to take issue with the leader of the opposition? There is no relationship whatever between the character of research that such an economic council as this might do and the character of research that is carried on by the national research council. One is deductive and the other inductive as I suggested to the right hon. gentleman yesterday. In the one field of research we experiment; we take for example the livers of one hundred dogs and treat them in different ways in the hope that we may find out something. We do not know before we start what the result will be; in that type of natural scientific research we have not necessarily the faintest conception as to what the result will be, but we just keep on experimenting, trying to find something. We may have an objective, and very often find something entirely different from that which we set out to find. This type of economic research is research that is based on the ascertaining of definite facts that will be admitted. The facts having first been admitted, conclusions are to be drawn by bringing those facts together in certain order or fashion and arguing to certain conclusions. The basis for economic research must be and will continue to be almost entirely statistical and therefore factual. The strength therefore of your statistical bureau will to an extent determine the success of the work of such an economic council as this is to be. I would suggest to the government in closing on this point that there are two matters to be taken into consideration: first, the general policy to which this council should devote its work and, second, the strengthening of the one body that
can make this work possible, the research council itself. The last clause of this bill provides for the fabling of reports each year by the secretary of the council, but the wording of that clause is altogether too slack. It states:
The secretary shall prepare an annual report to the minister with regard to the work of the council during the preceding year, which report shall he tabled in the House of Commons.
In my opinion the acting Prime Minister would ibe well advised to add the words "and findings" after the word "work," so that the house would be advised from time to time, as we are justified in requesting to be advised, as to the result of the research undertaken by this body on the questions it investigates during the year. I suggest most strongly that the amendment of the hon-. member for Wetaskiwin should be supported by the government and carried by the house.

In 1931 the United States government under President Hoover appointed a Senate committee to consider this same subject. The United States Senate is composed of big men. It is one of the greatest second chambers in the world. It has more legislative authority than any other second legislative chamber in the world. That Senate committee considered for some time, the subject of the establishment olf an economic council, and made a thorough and exhaustive survey, inviting to appear before them the most outstanding business men in the United States, the leading agriculturists, professors, labour men, and leading mem in all walks of life. After debating for several months they recommended to the government that an economic council should be ap= pointed. Whether that recommendation has been carried out I canniot now say definitely. What they did say iwas the objective of such a council:
We propose a national economic board, appointed by the president with the advice and consent of the Senate, and with preliminary advice from various national organizations. The members should represent special types of expert knowledge rather than special economic interests. They should include men expert in finance, scientific management, labour relations, economics, and agriculture or agricultural economics.
How if such a board is constituted with good intentions, as I believe is intended by this government, 1 cannot see how anything but benefit could result. All hon. members of this house give their best judgment, or they should, to the proposals that come before them for legislative action, recognizing that one of the principal purposes of governmental action is to provide employment for the citizens of the country. Having that in mind I cannot see how anything but benefit dan result from any government enrolling in support of the cabinet the ablest men obtainable from outside to give advice as to ways and means of providing employment for the citizens. Yet here we have this proposal received as if it were a joke. I deplore that attitude. As an ordinary business man I feel that members of this house should get down to the purpose for which they are here, and legislate in the interests of our people. Certainly
calling "Carried" to everything that comes up merely in order to get it through so that the session may be ended, in the expectation that there will be an early election, is not their purpose here. I will tell hon. gentlemen that the people of Canada are carefully scanning what goes on in this house; they are listening to what is being said here and they are not at all in accord with the attitude of the opposition who call "Carried" to most everything that comes up. Hon. gentlemen opposite will learn soon enough that there is to be an election this year; I am not a prophet but I will tell them that when the bell rings they will have a merry dance throughout the country.
In his remarks the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) became more or less mixed up; he started comparing this measure to the NRA. I spent some time in Washington when the NRA was up in congress; I also had conferences with a number of leading members of congress and of the senate, and I can say that this economic council is not at all an NRA matter, so why try to draw a red herring across the trail in order to promote opposition to a bill which I believe will be of some considerable benefit to the country. I am happy indeed to support this measure; I feel confident that when the government enrolls in its support or rather as a source of advice and information the able men it undoubtedly has in view, to meet with members of the cabinet and others on questions of business, of employment, of agriculture and of commerce, some good will be done which will benefit this country.

Economic Council
On the other hand the council should be free to make whatever recommendations the facts at their command warrant; they should be free to make the recommendations public, and then the government should take the responsibility for accepting or not accepting such recommendations. I believe firmly that if a carefully selected council, such as is here suggested and as will no doubt be appointed, were commissioned to find a way to distribute to the people of Canada the goods which those people can produce, such council could find a way to do it. It could, if it were left alone. Until we do have such a council and proceed on a basis of fact rather than on a basis of party tradition we will not find a solution for the problems with which we are confronted to-day. I would urge that the government change its mind in this regard. Such a change would ensure a better council than is now indicated; certainly it would not be a worse one. I do not see any common sense in a government taking the position that it will receive no suggestions from any outside people, and that the bill must go through exactly as it appears on its introduction, no matter how many improvements may be suggested. The government would not be harmed, indeed it would be helped, if the bill were improved as hon. members in this comer of the house have suggested. I again urge the leader of the government to reconsider the decision he has indicated to the house, and to allow hon. members at least to vote on the measure according to their individual ideas and not on party lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words concerning the bill, not because the explanation given by the acting Prime Minister lacked anything, but because I have been surprised this afternoon when I have listened to hon. members opposite ridicule the measure. I am in entire agreement with the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol) who s>poke only a few moments ago. We have before us a bill which hon. members opposite are attempting to ridicule out of court. Other bills which have been brought before this chamber and have been described as measures of progress and reform-the unemployment insurance bill, the eight hour day bill, and various others- hon. members opposite have tried to destroy, by declaring them unconstitutional. This measure they cannot prove unconstitutional, so they attempt to ridicule it out of court. If I may say so-and I am speaking as seriously as I have ever spoken in this chamber-to my mind this bill, far from being worthy of 92582-117
ridicule is the best measure we have introduced. I make that statement in all sincerity. The government has introduced progressive measures which may not have 'been as satisfactory as hon. members opposite or some hon. members in the third party might have desired. In that class we had the unemployment insurance bill, the eight hour day bill, and so on. No matter what may be said about them the fact remains that they were progressive measures, and were in line with present day world progress. I say the bill now before us is just as much in line with world progress, or even more, than the proposals contained in any other bill.
I remember, sir, that which apparently hon. members opposite seem to forget on all occasions, namely, that this world has been going through a period of crisis the like of which has never before been known. We have been going through an economic hurricane which has never been equalled. To-day that is but a platitude; every person admits it. Changed conditions require changed laws. The rest of the world absorbed that idea long before this; according to my information thirty-nine countries have instituted bodies similar to the one suggested in this measure. I admit quite freely that the bill may not make perfect law. After all, no government bringing in a measure expects perfection at the first attempt. I have no doubt imperfections will be found in it, and I have no doubt that some of the suggestions offered by hon. members in the third party, members who take a more constructive stand than do hon. members opposite-because their stand is entirely destructive-may ultimately be found necessary. I am free to make that admission. I must say, however, that some hon. members in the third party are destructive to a degree which does not serve them well and is not worthy of their ability. The hon. member for Bow River is notably one of those. He has an acute mind and a fine gift of speech, but I must say to him in a friendly spirit that the last few times he has discussed measures in this chamber he has adopted a destructive attitude not worthy of him and one which I believe will in the long run do him harm. For example, I will illustrate what I mean. To-day he finds fault with the whole bill because it is not perfect. I admit it is not perfect. I suggest that perhaps no two hon. members of the house would draw a bill in exactly the same language. But we must remember that the hon. member took the same attitude in regard to the unemployment insurance bill. Because it was not satisfactory to him and because

Economic Council

it did not embody certain ideas which he thought should be incorporated he voted against it. He and two other hon. members opposed the measure; I refer to the hon. members for Temiscouata and Labelle. I do not criticize them for voting against the measure; that is their privilege. I must say, however, that at a time like this, the position taken by the hon. member for Bow River, namely, that if he cannot have a bill passed one hundred per cent as he thinks it should be he will vote against it, is not worthy of his ability. I mention these points in a friendly way, and merely make the observation that his action does not constitute constructive criticism nor is it constructive in any way.
Hon. members opposite do not pretend to be constructive. In the last four or five years they have never pretended to be anything but destructive. For six sessions-and on many occasions they have referred to the fact that we have had six sessions-they have done nothing constructive. Their whole attitude has been one of fault finding and destructive criticism-nothing else. I do not expect better from them, but I do expect better from the hon. member for Bow River, a man of great ability and one who, for his own sake, I suggest might exercise a little more constructive effort, if he wishes to have legislation passed as he would like to have it.
The reason I felt impelled to speak was that I consider this to be one of the most constructive measures any Canadian government has brought forward. To-day we have such problems as unemployment-and I am laying aside the railways problem for the moment. Not only in Canada but in the world as a whole is there any problem which so urgently requires solution as that of unemployment. All hon. members would like to bring about a solution. If any hon. member-and I do not care who he might be- brought forward a solution of the unemployment problem, I believe I should support it, irrespective of the other members in the house. But so far, having read as widely as I am capable of reading, and having sought the ideas of other people, economists and others, I have not yet seen a solution for this very serious, critical and vital problem of all countries. We know that there is no solution at present because all countries are to-day suffering from it at least as severely as we are. The United States has twice as many unemployed as we have, and Great Britain more than we in proportion to population, and all the other countries of the world are faced with the same problem, and to a

greater degree in proportion to population than we are. Then let me suggest that a group of men such as is proposed in this bill, if they are given a problem such as that to consider, if they give their best brains to it as fifteen men of this type will do, may well succeed in bringing forth a settlement of such a vital problem to this country and to the world in general as unemployment.
There is the question of international trade. We all know that there has grown up economic nationalism throughout the world, which was really the basis of the calling together of the economic conference held in London a couple of years ago, and which really accomplished nothing. But there are methods by which economic nationalism may be decreased, and methods by which international trade may be increased.
There is the question of international debt, the question of interest payments which have been repudiated to a great extent by many of the countries which took part in the war. And finally perhaps the most urgent question of all, and one which is in a sense bound up with unemployment, is the question of the distribution of the products which we can produce in this country and which are produced by other countries. The countries in the world to-day have the ability to produce, if they could get down to business, more of food and clothing and shelter than is required by the peoples of the industrial countries of the world at any rate. But all the countries of the world have failed in working out anything in the shape of a method by which these products can be distributed. My hon. friends in the third party have taken a very strong atttiude on this question, and rightly so. I have done it myself out in the country, and all of us I believe, the best brains in the country, our best industrial brains, our business men and economists, must endeavour to work out some solution of that problem of distribution of the products of the farm, the factory, and the forest, which we are able to produce in the vast abundance of to-day.
May it not be that this economic council which we are setting up by this bill will, by sitting down and thinking over these problems, and studying them as members of the government have not time to do, bring forward some solution, for even one of the problems I have mentioned, and I have only touched the fringe of the many problems that can be dealt with by such a council.
This council is for economic research. It has already been pointed out by some speakers that there are two types of research. We have to-day a scientific research

Economic Council
council which is conducting research along scientific lines, by experiments in laboratories and so on. But the council that is proposed in this bill is an economic research council, a council which will study social and economic laws with the object of solving those problems which have arisen because there is something wrong in the whole social and economic system of Canada and other countries. It has been pointed out by the right hon. gentleman who introduced this bill that this council is for the purpose of inquiry and report, for the purpose of advising the government and advising this parliament and indeed the people of this country. It has no governing authority. This same type of advisory council has been established in nearly all the progressive countries of the world. I made it my business while the debate was going on to look up a list of the countries which have established some such council as this. 'Germany has what they call a federal economic council; Italy a national council of corporations; France and Belgium, a national economic council, and Czechoslovakia, Spain, Japan, Chile, China and even Russia have some such council as this which we are proposing to set up. My hon. friends laugh. Some of my hon. friends in the far corner sometimes point to Russia as one of the proofs of failure in this country. I think Russia at any rate has had the sense which apparently the official opposition and some of my friends in the far corner do not seem to have, of setting up an economic council of this sort. Great Britain since 1930 has had an economic advisory council, and its purposes have been described as follows:
To advise His Majesty's government in economic matters, to make continuous study of developments in trade and industry and in the use of national and imperial resources ... and of all aspects of national, imperial and international economy with a bearing on the prosperity of the country.
That is exactly the purpose of this council. It will study the problems which the government of the day or parliament desires to submit to it.
The United States has a council of economic research. It is a private body, supported by private donations. Altogether there are 39 different countries of the world which have established such a council as this. Surely then it is not a strange thing that Canada should be the fortieth country to do it. Surely we are not to be ridiculed and laughed at if we set up a council which 39 other countries, most of them greater in population than us and many of them richer, have already set up. Here is a council to be composed 92582-1174
of seven government officials, five men from economic bodies, and three experts.
May I just say here, as one who has been in this house for a great many years, that I do not believe this parliament or this government or previous governments have made sufficient use of the very outstanding ability which we possess in the civil service of this country. In my opinion we have talked too much about the boundless ability and brilliance of the civil service in other countries, such as England particularly, and in that way unconsciously we have belittled our own civil service. I want to say here publicly to-day that in my opinion our civil service is equal to any civil service in any other country of the world. We have in this country a civil service which during the imperial economic conference held in Ottawa in 1932 so ably organized the arrangements and work of that conference that it was stated by those who attended it that never in the history of imperial conferences had the organization been so ably done. That is only an illustration. All of us can name able civil servants. We have able deputy ministers, and heads of branches of departments who are outstandingly able men, leaders in their particular field. Then is it a mistake to take seven of these well qualified officials, say the head of the statistical branch, deputy ministers and experts, and put them on a council and ask them to work together instead of working as they do at present more or less in opposition to each other? Is it a thing to be ridiculed that we ask seven of them to link up their activities with those of three heads of economic bodies, labour unions, if you like, and manufacturing associations-I am giving these thoughts just as they occur to me, Mr. Chairman, just thinking out loud-and assisted by three experts? Is the government to be ridiculed because it has had the wisdom to do what thirty-nine other governments have done? Surely my hon. friends opposite have not thought over this sufficiently or they would not take the attitude of endeavouring to kill this proposal by ridicule, just as they have endeavoured to kill by constitutional argument a number of the other reform measures of the government. Over and over again as the government has brought forward its reform measures they have shown that they are opposed to them and they have tried to make them look ridiculous, but they have finally voted for them, except the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who had the courage to vote against the unemployment insurance measure. And they will not vote against this measure. They are trying instead to kill it by kindness, to behead it by ridi-
Economic Council

cule. Their attitude is: We are all for this, but we want to chop off its head. That is not killing, according to their point of view. I trust that my hon. friends will be able to see as clearly as I do the importance of an economic body such as this, which it has been found well to set up in thirty-nine other countries of the world, Canada making the fortieth. I suggest that they do not take the attitude of belittling an organization such as this which can certainly do no harm, and to my mind must inevitably do some good for the people of this country and for the government and parliament of Canada.

My hon. friend suggests that because all ills have not been cured, no effort should be made to cure them. speechtext:
I do not
oppose this bill and have not done so; what I have pointed out is that it was a pallid ghost of what we in this corner had sought, and no possible mistake can be made in the statement that the government in bringing in this legislation did not introduce it in accordance with the recommendations that had come from this corner of the house. When) the stream of irrepressible and ebullient verbosity of the Minister of Railways flows on, one is swept away by the torrent of words in which he engulfs his opponents, and while fluency is one of the qualities that I admire most in him, I have a sensation of drowning as I listen to him. But may I suggest that his illustrations were not well chosen. This bill is not patterned after the German method. It would not be so bad a bill if it were. Nor is it patterned after the Russian method, in spite of what the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) said. It is not patterned on any European model at all; it is patterned definitely after the Japanese model. May I give to hon. members of the committee the set-up in Japan for precisely such an economic council.
Symptoms of a state of crisis became noticeable in Japan soon after the end of the war; the increasing population, which made an extension of production and social welfare work necessary, brought economic problems into the foreground and made it appear desirable that persons of experience in these matters should participate in the life of the state.

Economic Council
This government is just becoming aware now of the fact that someone else beyond the government should participate in the life of the state.
An economic council was consequently appointed for the empire in 1924-
We are now in 1935.
-by imperial decree No. 70 of April 1st. Unlike the German Reich economic council, which, as a then unique attempt to establish an organic economic organization, aroused much interest and indeed gave rise to imitation in other countries, the Japanese imperial economic council was dependent, as one of the first economic institutions, on the prime minister. At the request and on the instructions of the ministers for agriculture and for trade and for finance-
It is even broader than this measure.
-and not therefore on its own initiative, it was to give opinions with regard to questions affecting the furtherance of national economy. It is, indeed, empowered itself to put forward proposals-
Which this proposed council is not empowered to do.
-with regard to matters within this sphere. This provision might, in practice, be interpreted in such a manner as to extend its rights further than the law suggests; it would be of interest to examine its activities in this direction.
I suggest that the government would be well advised to reconsider its position in this matter. A Review of the Economic Councils in the Different Countries of the World, by Doctor Elli Lindner, published by the League of Nations, points out that the economic councils in existence fall into two groups, the first group comprising those of France, Germany and Italy, which, being formed on the basis of a wide representation of economic circles, have an effective influence on national economic policy. They possess the right of initiative, and cooperate in preparing bills of an economic character before they are submitted to parliament for approval. Now that is quite a different sort of thing from this proposal. This is an emaciated, stupid, silly modification; it is a fleshless skeleton, nothing but a skeleton. When the hon. member for Wetaskiwin and others try to put a little flesh and muscle on it and develop a mind in it their suggestions are received only with lectures from the treasury benches and a torrent of words that bear no relation whatever to the facts or show evidence of study of the problem. The report continues:
There is, however, a fundamental difference between the French and' German economic councils and the council of corporations. Whereas the two former bodies confine themselves to strictly advisory functions, the
Italian council of corporations can in certain circumstances take decisions, though its powers are, generally speaking, limited by the right of veto held by the prime minister.
The second group, which is much the larger, includes a number of various 'bodies consisting of economic experts or representatives of various professions invited by the government-
As in this case.
-or by a member of the government to give their opinions on questions affecting the national economy generally or on special questions a study of which is of particular interest to the economic life of the country.
This bill belongs to the latter group. Now, while there have been economic councils of these two types in operation for many years, none of them has succeeded in solving the problem-not one of them. And they will not do so, because the directional policy in every single case has not been of a kind calculated to lead to a solution of a problem that cannot be solved under the present capitalist system. I am quite willing that the government should seek advice. I am glad it is providing itself with a crab apple since it does not want a Delicious or a McIntosh. But let it not delude either itself or the country; this economic council will not solve the problem, because the direction of it inevitably will be of the character of the government itself, and it will direct its efforts towards the stabilizing of conditions as they are in so far as they can be stabilized. That is, they will keep everything of the present system that they possibly can keep and make it operate. But it is a futile and vain attempt to make the unworkable work and is bound to fail, just as every economic council although long established has failed. But I welcome it because, if it is properly constituted, if it is composed of men of the type of mind I hope it will be, it may in time result in directing the attention of the government to the blind alley in which it finds itself.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION OP BODY TO COORDINATE WORK OF DEPARTMENTS AND TO INVESTIGATE AND ADVISE UPON SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Clause 6 is the most important clause of this bill, as it relates to the duties of the council. The people of this country are paying to-day for thirty years' neglect of this problem. The government has brought down a most important bill for social and economic reform. The proposal for this legislation came from the Conservative opposition away back in 1923 in connection with the question of a national coal supply. To-day I have a return showing that 2,800,000 tons of coal were moved last year from the maritime provinces to central Canada as a result of that proposal. Then this policy came up again some years afterwards, in 1928 and again in 1930, and what did the government of that
Economic Council

time do? I shall read their reply to a question which I asked the government on March 13, 1930, with reference to an advisory economic committee along the lines of this bill. I asked:
Will the government consider the appointment of an advisory economic committee for Canada to deal with economic questions?
And the reply of the Prime Minister of the day was:
This and kindred subjects are receiving the attention of the government.
But they received no attention whatever, with the result that hundreds of millions of dollars were voted to the Canadian National Railways. Had that policy been adopted back in 1928 millions and millions of dollars would have been saved to the taxpayers of the country in over-capitalization and over-government. Looking over those years we see that no study was made of the question of unemployment, seasonal, technological or cyclical; no study was made by any federal, provincial or municipal body of the inroads being made by science and the machine on the employment of labour. The same thing is true of the housing question. Public works were constructed that had no economic value; some of them will never pay the fixed charges or the debt charges on them. Our natural resources have been given away; during the past thirty years our natural resources of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mine were given away in a haphazard manner and the people are suffering for it to-day. Then look at the power situation-a country so rich in power as Canada, with forty-two million potential horsepower and only seven million developed, and no effort looking to a national hydro power policy. No study at all was made of these questions, nor of the inroads into the earnings of our steam railways made by motor buses and truck freight traffic.
When we look over these problems we see the necessity of a body such as this, Mr. Chairman, and I appeal to the opposition to help the government pull the country out of the mire. I do not think we should depend on the federal government to do everything. Canada's national economic problems are not going to be solved by majorities in parliament; they call for wide national sacrifices and the support not only of the government of the day and the opposition but also of churches, boards of trade and all public bodies. While this body is advisory, if its services are properly utilized it may result in untold good to the people of this country, who have become aware as never before of the economic abuses that are carried on here. It has been argued that

parliamentary control has been so successful in education and finance, so why not extend it to banking and commerce, unemployment, housing, agriculture, imports and exports, radio and everything else from Dan to Beersheba? In the past we have had government commissions and departments multiplied to an unparalleled extent, not only in federal but also in provincial and municipal affairs, and I believe one of the principal problems that should be taken up by this council is the coordination of the problems of our various federal, provincial and municipal governments. If they only accomplish that task, so that we need not rely on some body away over in Geneva to solve our problems, they will do a great work. Some of these difficulties have been met by the municipalities themselves by way of contract; I refer to the problems in connection with fair wages, minimum wages, eight hour day, the elimination of sweat shops and child labour.
It seems to me that the principal fault of our parliamentary system under the British North America Act is that so far as our parliamentary institutions are concerned Canada is well on the way to being upside down. I think this council should consider parliamentary and constitutional reform such as will enable this country to solve its own problems. The question of the constitution of Canada is a matter to which I think the government should give very careful consideration. In the past we have derived very little benefit from some of our commissions because they have been top heavy with university professors and economists. If we want to do something practical we will have to rely on others than economists. Political economy is all right in its way, but it is not an exact science like medicine, chemistry or biology. These scientists argue from facts; the economist does not do so. He gives his opinion, and the opinions of economists are as far apart as the poles. So I hope this council will include some practical men ; I think in reality it should be a brain trust to help solve some of the problems of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mine. Professors are all very well in universities so long as they stick to their last, but many of them give advice on matters with which they are not familiar, and we have had a great deal of advice of that type. I think it would be better to get some practical business men together with the permanent officials, because when all is said and done the backbone of any government is the permanent staff, who carry on work that cannot be carried on by anyone else.

Economic Council
This council might well take up the question of what is to be done in regard to suitable employment for boys and girls of high school age, say up to eighteen. No study of that question has been made by any body so far as I can find out. I think they might study, investigate and report as to what should be done, in conjunction with the provinces and the municipalities, to solve that problem. To-day the youth of our country are suffering as never before. The commission might also make a study of industry. Low wages in Canada have been proved to be the cause of much crime in this country. Many children who are working in factories should be in schools, and the records show that most of our young offenders are underprivileged children, many of them from poverty stricken homes, who have been undernourished and handicapped and who have never had a chance or a steady job. So I think this body might make a report on what might be done along that line.
I believe another matter which might be taken up by this council, together with departmental officials, is the question of the evasion of our income tax by big business supermen, and trusts and high finance, in relation to unemployment. A commission in the United States studied this problem on Wall street and found that such evasion was retarding industry and trade in that country. The commission found that this led to starving industry and to very serious unemployment and was the cause of many of the evils from which that country was suffering. In my opinion income tax returns should be made public and I hope that when this council is set up it will go into that question. The brain trust in the United States, in attacking that problem, did more to help unemployment by exposing big business than was done by any other agency. In my opinion this council could do no better service than to recommend the publication of all income tax returns. We publish the facts and they are an open book in connection with sales of real estate and chattel mortgages and bills of sale, so why should we not publish the facts in connection with some in this country who are hoarding wealth and evading the payment of income tax with their financial manipulations. I believe that is one of the most important things that might be dealt with by this advisory body. There has been some talk of a union government in this country. In my humble opinion we had enough of that kind of government. Further, I believe the coordination of our two railways is impossible; I think with expanding trade and
the end of the depression the national railways will become a great asset to Canada.
Ini conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I believe this to be the most important matter to come before parliament this session. There are those in this country who, having seen the economic waste that has gone on in connection with our resources, have laid the blame on our parliamentary and constitutional system. I think one of the most important matters that might be taken up by this advisory body would be some recommendation as to the reorganization of our parliamentary and constitutional system so as to bring it more up to date, in order that we may deal with some of these economic problems quickly in a practical and modern way. At the present time the British North America Act, as we have it, is a danger to the well being of the country. I do not think we should pass on problem after problem to different public bodies, which piles up delay after delay; we should have a quick, modern way of solving our difficulties. It is this situation that prompts some Canadians to long for a dictator in this country; they see the evils which have been apparent to parliament for many years, with parliament doing nothing to check them. I might refer to the terrible condition of agricultural and railway workers and those in the mines, as well as those in industry. We as a parliament must not forget that these citizens have invested their lives in these industries, but today they are suffering because of the selfishness of some of those who are styled big business. If we are to have a brain trust now let us have some proper investigation, something like the investigation of Wall Street by the United States senate. Let us have an investigation in the same way of St. James Street, and the way big business has been responsible for some of the very evils that we hope1 to cure through legislation of this kind. Let us have a real inquiry. If the investigation I proposed in 1923, 1928 and 1930 for an economic council for Canada had been made there would have been no Beauharnois deal. The natural resources the Lord gave' us in the St. Lawrence river and in the Ottawa river were intended not for the barons of St. James Street, but for all His creatures in the country. When I proposed that we should have an inquiry in connection with the national coal supply I was told by the head of the National railways, right in the committee which had been appointed, that I was proposing a bargain lunch counter system of freight rates to carry the coal from the maritimes and Alberta to central Canada.
Economic Council

In 1823, 1928 and 1930 I asked the government of the day to appoint a body such as is now suggested, and we know what the reply was at that time. They did nothing, despite the fact that such a council had been appointed in England in the fall of 1928, and the present measure is patterned after their act. Clause 6 of this bill is almost the same as one of the clauses in the British act. The fact that they did do this is one of the chief reasons why the mother country has recovered faster than any other country. Look at what they are doing by way of supplying themselves with food. Some time ago they could not in a year produce more than a month's supply at one time, but to-day they are going over every lot and every farm in England and are making a great effort to increase their food supply to the point where they will not be dependent upon outside countries as much as they were. The farmers of Canada will not enljoy the market they used bo have in the old country. They investigated the coal and steel industries, and as a result a report was made to the British parliament in 1928. Effect was given to the report; they did not do as we do in Canada. When our officials make a report it is pigeonholed. Their report was adopted, and all sections of the country, including the church, boards of trade and labour organizations have got together to pull the country out of the mire. That is what we need in Canada, and what we would have had if the suggestion made in 1928 had been adopted by the government of that day.
Mr. MacINNffiS:	I 'believe the house
should thank the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Irvine) and also the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) for changing the proceedings from a farce to a serious consideration of an important problem. This measure should receive serious consideration. If any person does not believe it should be given serious thought then I suggest that person should oppose it and should not attempt to ridicule it.
Why is there a necessity for an economic council? Why do we find governments in many countries appointing councils of this kind? That is one of the first questions we should ask ourselves. To my mind the answer is this:	In the past, because of certain conditions, private interests were able to take care of the economic and social conditions within a country. During the last few years, however, and particularly since the beginning of the depression, private enterprise has fallen down and is no longer able to take care of the economic matters which at one time

it attended to. Private enterprise always had at its command technical advisers, economic advisers, financial advisers and men qualified to give other kinds of advice. If governments are to be called upon to do the work which at one time was done by private enterprise, then governments will have to have officials at their command. Because the government of Canada, like the governments of other countries, have so many problems to consider, I believe they should have experts at their command who would be able to give sound advice. Some hon. members, and particularly the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), referred to the many problems confronting Canada-unemployment, railways, transportation, trade, and finance. The suggestion was made that we should try to find a solution for these problems. In my opinion the mistake made by the Minister of Railways and Canals and by other hon. members is that of believing that these difficulties can be solved one by one. As a matter of fact these different problems are not causes; they are effects. They are conditions which have arisen out of the fundamental basis of our whole economic and social life. When you have solved unemployment you have solved at the same time the problems of trade, transportation and finance. They are linked together and one cannot be solved without solving the others.
There is only one problem which has always confronted the people of the world, and it is that of deciding how best to provide themselves with food, clothing and shelter; that problem settled we find that others fall into line and are merely detail. The problem of providing food, clothing and shelter has confronted the human race from the time of its first appearance on earth up to the present day, the only difference being that to-day we have within our grasp or at our command the means to solve the problem once and fo-r all. I believe it was the Prime Minister who said some few years ago in this chamber that at that time-and of course the same condition obtains to-day -there was in Canada industrial equipment sufficient to meet the needs of 25,000,000 people. To-day our population is only a little more than 10,000,000 people, and I submit that if we have the equipment to supply the needs of 25,000,000 people it should be somebody's business to find why we cannot use our wealth to meet the needs of our citizens. If the economic council will do that, then surely it is worth while. I must say however that I would be opposed to an economic council of which the present Prime

Economic Council
Minister would be the chairman, not because I have not a high regard for his ability, integrity and honesty, but because I feel that during the last five years he has dominated his cabinet, possibly to the detriment of legislation which has come before us. I am sure that in the same way he would dominate a council, particularly one made up in greater part of civil servants.
The point was made that we had never made use of our civil service. As a matter of fact we have never made full use of any of our resources, and if this economic council could show us how to make use not only of our civil servants but of our natural resources, our industrial equipment and our man power, both mentally and physically, then the legislation would be worth while. I would suggest again that the government consider seriously the amendment proposed by the hon. .member for Wetaskiwin. Although as drafted it may not meet with their approval I believe they should hold it over and ascertain whether or not they could bring down an amendment which would be more to their liking and would also meet the purposes for which the amendment was intended.

To-day it is common to hear the statement that the problem of production has been solved. That of course is only a comparative statement, but the efficiency of the productive system is so far ahead of our methods of distribution that it seems to me there is every reason for saying that the problem of distribution is the greatest one facing us to-day. In my humble opinion there is no reason why the government should not accept the amendment offered by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). Our scientists and engineers have gone a long way in solving the problem of production. In Canada we have over eight million horsepower of mechanical energy installed in factories and power houses. Coupled with splendid labour saving machinery we have now a production system with power behind it which is equal to the .power of eighty million slaves, to work for this nation of ten million people. We can produce goods in abundance, food, clothing, and shelter for more people than we have here, and yet we continue to endure this condition of poverty in the midst of plenty.
In 1929, so we have been told, we entered upon a period of depression due to the fact that we had produced too much. Surely it should not be necessary to say anything more than that to convince the government and members of this committee that this problem of distribution is the great one facing us. I
remember four years ago the president of one of our banks said that the depression was caused by overproduction, and he was followed a few minutes later by the general manager who said in his speech that the way out was to work harder. Now if this depression was caused by overproduction, we all know surely that we cannot get out of it by working harder and producing more. Surely the only solution is greater consumption. There is the important problem facing us. How can we get that system which will enable us as a people to consume what we now produce? I say again that is the greatest problem facing us, that of finding a better system of distribution, and I do not see why we should not state in this act that one of the duties to be undertaken by this board, which is to be called an economic council and is to advise the government, shall be to consider this problem of distribution. I certainly hope that the government will change their attitude and accept the amendment that has been offered by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot let the vote take .place without saying a word in support of the amendment which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). The bill as it stands is distinctly a step in the right direction, and I shall take pleasure in supporting it, but I do not think it goes far enough. It does not really meet what is probably the most important situation facing us, and that is the problem of purchasing power, and that I believe was the idea of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin in putting forward his amendment. No doubt the bill is being introduced to-day for no other reason than that of the extraordinary situation in which this country now finds itself. We are wealthy in the matter of goods and services, but financially we are poor. There is certainly a contradiction. It seams to me that we have been thinking too much both in the past and in the present in terms of money. We do not think sufficiently in terms of goods and services. The very fact that to-day we have on the one hand such vast quantities of goods everywhere, and the possibility of producing so much more, while at the same time we have more poverty, throughout this country than we have had for many years, should be a challenge to every thinking member of this house. We have an army of somewhere around five hundred thousand people unemployed, and we are keeping to-day at the expense of the federal government no less than one million people on relief. These are some of the reasons no doubt why the government
Economic Council

has introduced this legislation and I congratulate them upon doing so. I do feel, however, that if they refuse to accept the amendment now before us simply because it has been proposed by a private member of this house, they are making a great mistake.
May I remind this house that whatever is physically possible is or should be financially possible, and that is one of the problems that the amendment suggests should be considered. The condition in which we find ourselves to-day, with this vast amount of poverty, is largely the secret of many of our other problems. The railway problem, for instance, is largely brought about because of a lack of purchasing power on the part of the people. If -people had purchasing power they would travel a great deal more than they do to-day, and would provide freight and express business for our railways, and we would not have the railway deficits that face us every year. Just about twelve months ago the railways of Canada put on reasonable rates from western Canada to the east, and they had to put on several extra trains to accommodate the people who wanted to come east. The people wanted to travel in any case, and they did travel then because they could travel at much lower rates.
The health problem again can be laid largely at the door of poverty. When people are in poverty they cannot get the necessaries of life, with the result that they are forced to adopt a lower standard of living, and ill health often develops. Crime also can largely be laid at the door of poverty because everybody recognizes that poverty is the mother of crime.
