Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38, to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain).
He said: This is now the fourth time I have introduced this matter into the house by way of a bill. The first year I came here I introduced it by way of a resolution. I have no apologies to offer to the house and to the country for keeping at this matter for four years; indeed, I intend to carry on with the fight as long as I am a member.
Long ago I came to the conclusion that it is within the House of Commons that this matter, the fight that British Columbia has in connection with the equalization of freight rates, should be fought out.
It is not my intention again to go into every phase of the question, because I am of opinion that after some four years perhaps enough has been said regarding the various rates and the rate structure without again taking up the time of the house in connection with them. However I would like to take a few moments to touch briefly on the history of the case as it affects the province of British Columbia.
Shortly, the situation is this: British Columbia at the time of confederation was a crown colony. Portions of railway systems had been constructed in Eastern Canada, but no outlet or access to the Pacific coast by railroad was then in existence. British Columbia at that time had her own customs and excise and was under the British crown a self-governing colony. As an inducement for her to give up those privileges and to join with the other provinces in order to complete this country as a dominion, she consented to do so on the understanding that railway connection would be given her and also that she would be placed on an equality with the other provinces so far as transportation was concerned.
The dominion government then had surveyors map out a route into British Columbia
Railway Act

Rates on Grain

and they se'icted what is known as the Yellow-head pass route. The Canadian Pacific Railway were induced-and I am just stating the facts briefly-to undertake to build that railway into British Columbia. They however put their own surveyors on the work and decided that they would take another route which they declared was some one hundred and forty-two miles shorter, and known as the Kicking Horse pass route. After the railway was constructed, the rates into that province were set and the Canadian Pacific Railway at that time took the stand that as some difficulties had been encountered in regard to the construction of that road, necessitating heavy blasting of rock and so forth, they were entitled to charge higher rates than were being charged in other parts of the dominion. It must be remembered that at that time the Crowsnest pass rates were in existence. The people of British Columbia felt greatly incensed at the attitude of the Canadian Pacific, because they had been given to understand that they would be placed on an equal basis as to rates with the people of the other provinces. It is without prejudice that I say this: The attitude of the Canadian Pacific themselves in those early days largely brought about the construction of a second road into that province. British Columbia in 1909 or 1910 decided that something had to be done to counteract the power of the Canadian Pacific Railway and to give that corporation some competition by way of another railway in an endeavour to bring the rates down. So we had constructed from Edmonton to Vancouver another line which now is comprised within the Canadian National railway system. When the railway was being built, the people of British Columbia were taking care that they would have control of the rates and as matter of fact were considering inserting the rates in the act, but they did not go so far as that. However they saw to it that in the Railway Act passed in the session of 1909-10, the government of British Columbia would control completely the rates of that railway. But what happened? Just after the line was completed, the dominion parliament passed an act to the effect that that railway was for the general good of Canada, and at one fell swoop, shall I say, took away the railroads laid down by British Columbia and placed them under the board of railway commissioners. That very briefly is an outline of the history of the matter. I am not going to take up the time of the house with every little detail because I have many other matters to speak of, and as I said before, many of these facts have been placed on the 
records of previous years. The board of railway commissioners, might I point out, was presumably set up as a safeguard for the people; that is fairly evident I believe, because the railroads themselves required no safeguards as to rates. The railroads could set the rates, but as a safeguard so that the railroads would confine themselves to reasonable rates, a board known as the board of railway commissioners was set up, and I think I am correct when I state that that board was set up with the view principally of protecting the people from both railroads and not the railways from the people.
I am of opinion that the time has now come to review the board of railway commissioners. We have had put through this house an act to bring about compulsory cooperation in both railways. If I may use that term, and there is no doubt that competition in rates to capture traffic has been to a certain extent, if not entirely, eliminated. When one considers that in the neighbourhood of $330,000 annually is paid out to that board, that competition has largely been eliminated, and we are living in the year of our Lord 1935, under changed conditions, I think it would be well for this parliament to consider whether the board of railway commissioners is fulfilling as useful a function as it did when it was first set up.
The three most important factors in connection with the cost of railway service are construction, operation and maintenance. I am not going into the question of finance and all the intricacies of railroad management; I speak simply of the three principal items determining the cost of railway service. I have stated many times, and repeat briefly without going into minute detail, that in British Columbia construction costs were lower than they were in many other parts of eastern and central Canada; and also in that province they have lower operation costs and lower costs of maintenance. I repeat that, because it does annoy one to be told by some people that the railroads there have the mountain grades to overcome. We have, as is well known in British Columbia, the lowest grades in the whole dominion, especially through the Yellowhead pass from Edmonton, over the Canadian National, the maximum grade being seven-tenths of one per cent. I say again that the construction costs, the operation costs, and the maintenance costs of both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National in the province of British Columbia are comparable with the low costs

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
on the prairie and much lower than in parts of eastern Canada, especially over the Laurentian range.
British Columbia has paid very dearly for the mistake made by the Canadian Pacific in taking the Kicking Horse pass route. Although the Canadian Pacific received large grants of land and large subsidies as well to meet their contention that they had these difficulties to overcome, rates were set having in view the grades on that line at that time, and those rates have been maintained right up to the present day and have cost the people of British Columbia many millions of dollars more than they ought to have paid. I stated last session and I repeat that British Columbia can never look for any redress from the board of railway commissioners unless greater powers are given that board and drastic changes made as well. I pointed out last year that it was useless to go before that board. In spite of that, however, I was willing to try out the board, and so made an appeal to them asking that feed grains and mill feeds be carried to British Columbia at the same rate for domestic use as for export. Without going too deeply into the matter I may say briefly that the board relied in its judgment almost entirely on past judgments, at least the majority judgment did. The question was raised at the outset of the appeal whether I had any right to be there, inasmuch as the question had been decided some years ago. Right at the start the railway companies objected, saying this was the same appeal, and they asked the board not to listen to it. They said there would be no end to it if this case were again opened up. But the application I had before the board of railway commissioners was not entirely the same as the former one, because I was asking only that feed grains and mill feeds be carried into that province at the same rate as that charged on the same commodities for export.
To show how difficult it is to interpret a statement of the principles that should guide the board I am going to read the order in council, P.C. 886, passed in 1925, from which I ask hon. members if they would not form the opinion that very wide powers were given to the board to equalize rates. It says:
The committee are of the opinion that the policy of equalization of freight rates should' be recognized to the fullest possible extent as being the only means of dealing equitably with all parts of Canada and as being the method best calculated to facilitate the interchange of commodities between the various portions of
the dominion, as well as the encouragement of industry and agriculture and the development of export trade.
The committee are further of the opinion that to give effect to this policy, and considering the submissions made by counsel and important trade organizations representing different provinces and localities in the dominion as to the disadvantages that would be suffered by such provinces or localities by any partial or incomplete consideration of the freight rate structure, a thorough and complete investigation of the whole subject of railway freight rates in the dominion should be carried out by the board of railway commissioners, the body constituted by parliament with full powers under statute to fix and control railway rates.
The committee are further of the opinion that as the production and export of grain and flour forms one of the chief assets of the dominion, and in order to encourage the further development of the great grain growing provinces of the west^ on which development the future of Canada in large measure depends, it is desirable that the maximum cost of the transportation of these products should be determined and known, and therefore are of the opinion that the maximum established for rates on grain and flour, as at present in force under the Crowsnest pass agreement, should not be exceeded.
The ordinary layman reading that would, I think, be inclined to believe that wide instructions were given to the board of railway commissioners to equalize freight rates and for the conduct of that inquiry. That is why I stated at the beginning of my address this evening that if the province of British Columbia is ever to obtain any redress from the board of railway commissioners, drastic changes will have to be made in the Railway Act, and it would have to be stated explicitly. Otherwise, from the experience I have had and the judgments which have been rendered, I am convinced that the board would go through the act with a fine tooth comb to see if they could evade the question so far as the people are concerned. I was told last year, I believe by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), that the House of Commons is not the place to fix railway rates. I quite agree that if one brought into the House of Commons the whole railway rate structure of this dominion there might be some kind of a mix-up. But I say this, and I say it from experience, that parliament could not do worse than what is in existence at the present- time. I ask any hon. member to look at the various rates in existence from one end of this country to the other and then consider whether parliament could have done any worse than the railways and the board of railway commissioners have done. But, Mr. Speaker, we are not asking parliament to fix all freight rates; we are asking parliament to give British Columbia what has been denied
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

that province since 1886, and what was given the other portions of this dominion. We are not asking for anything unfair; we are not asking for lower rates than are given other provinces. We are asking for the same equal treatment that has been accorded the other provinces and surely that is within our rights; surely that is not unfair. We are asking this from, the court of last resort, the highest court in the land, which is the parliament of Canada.
I am going to quote just one or two rates to show what I call the hodge-podge of railway rates in this country. One could devote a whole evening to these rates, but I am going to quote only a few. I want first to show the house the penalty British Columbia has to pay when it ships produce east as compared with other provinces when they ship the same produce west. If British Columbia wants to ship butter to Calgary or Edmonton the rate is $1.49 per hundred pounds, while if Calgary or Edmonton want to ship buitber to Vancouver they pay only $137 per hundred pounds. What is the reason for the difference? Then take eggs: British Columbia produces great quantities of eggs; so does Alberta. But when we ship our eggs to Calgary or Edmonton we are charged $1.13 per hundred pounds while if Calgary or Edmontoni ship eggs to us they pay only $1.10. The same situation exists in regard to fresh beef; the rate from Vancouver to Calgary or Edmonton is $1.13 per hundred pounds while the rate from Calgary or Edmonton to Vancouver is $1.10. Cattle shipped from Vancouver to Calgary or Edmonton pay 57^ cents per hundred poupds while cattle going from Edmonton or Calgary to Vancouver pay 56 cents per hundred pounds. It would be just as reasonable if the railway companies charged their passengers one rate from Calgary or Edmonton to Vancouver and another rate when returning from Vancouver back to Calgary or Edmonton. No railway company and no government would stand for any such differences in passenger fares, but the different freight rates I have quoted have been in existence for many years.
One might go on and show just how much more British Columbia is paying than is being paid by the other provinces, and I would point out that British Columbia should receive greater consideration from the eastern provinces because, as is well known to every hon. member from British Columbia at least, that province buys most of its manufactured articles in the protected east, but it is compelled to sell all its own commodities on a world market. But no consideration has been given that province in connection with the

shipment of such commodities as butter, eggs, fresh beef, cattle and so on. I am not going to raise any question of the east against the west or the west against the east, nor am I criticizing ithe eastern provinces; but I would point out that all the rates in the eastern provinces are far lower than the rates in the west. I will mention just one or two. The eastern carload rate for a two hundred mile haul is 15 cents per hundred pounds; the less than carload rate is 30i cents. In the west those rates are 20 cents and 51 cents, while in the Pacific section they are 23 cents and 59 cents. I have a whole list of such comparisons but I am not going to put them on record because it would take too much time. Looking over that list, however, one must come to the conclusion that the eastern provinces and central Canada certainly enjoy far lower rates than those in force in ithe province of British Columbia. After all, Mr. Speaker, provided that conditions are the same and that maintenance and construction costs are roughly the same, mile for mile should not we in the province of British Columbia have the same rates as apply in other parts of the dominion?
I have heard some criticism in regard to the Crowsnest pass rates, for example. I do not think the government however would assume the responsibility of removing those rates, which were set by statute in 1897 and reaffirmed1 by parliament in 1925 with some changes. It is unfortunate that in 1925, when the change took place, those rates were not extended to British Columbia, but I do not think this Or any other government would care to assume the responsibility of saying the Crowsnest pass rates were too low or unfair. There they are, and I claim that we in British Columbia are just as much entitled to those rates as are the central and eastern provinces. I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that one of the things wrong with our railways is that the passenger system is too costly. I believe a large part of the railway losses in this country occurs in connection with the passenger traffic. The railways were built primarily for freight, but the freight end of the business has not been developed as it should have 'been. I do not believe any hon. member would suggest that passenger rates should be raised; no, the tendency is to lower them in order to induce people to travel. The same principle should apply in connection with freight. To-day the railways are complaining of competition from other methods of transportation. I think they are going to have even more competition of that kind. They are experiencing it now on tile great lakes, and

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
in various parts of the country they are suffering from the competition of the trucks. I predict that if railway rates to British Columbia are not lowered, once the highway is completed from the prairies to British Columbia we will see long lines of trucks hauling wheat and other produce between these points because they can do it for much less than what is charged by the railways. Two years ago they tried moving apples from the Okanagan valley by trucks; last year many carloads of apples were trucked along the highway from Okanagan valley which in past years had been handled by the railways. Why is that being done? It is because the railways refuse to alter or lower their rates. The consuming public are not interested in the intricacies of freight rates; what they want is cheap service and if the motor trucks can offer them a cheap service that is the kind of transportation they are going to patronize.
Coming to the export rate to British Columbia, which is twenty cents per hundred pounds for export, might I point out that while on the surface it would appear that this is comparable to the rate to Fort William, it is really still much higher than that rate. During the hearing of the matter I challenged the railways to prove to the board of railway commissioners that the export rate on grain was a losing rate, I take the stand that the rate of twenty cents is a paying rate, and if that is so, why should the people of British Columbia who want to use wheat have to pay twice the rate charged on other grain that is hauled in the same trains by the same engines over the same tracks and in charge of the same crews? There is no reason for it at all. The railway companies have always dodged the issue when confronted with the statement that the export rate is a paying rate. The hauling of wheat is one of the major traffic items of the railways, and this might interest some hon. members:	During the past few years the
great bulk of Canadian wheat has been going out through Pacific coast outlets. In 1933 over 100,000,000 bushels of wheat went through the Pacific coast outlets while a total of only 83,000,000 bushels went out through all the eastern Canadian ports. I received these figures to-day, and to me they were most interesting. Of the 83,000,000 bushels shipped through the eastern ports over 6,000,000 bushels were from the United States. The exact figure for the Pacific coast ports is 100,587,923 bushels and for the combined eastern ports including grain from the #2582-118
United States, 83,675,534 bushels. I believe these figures will indicate the trend of the grain traffic to-day.
May I point out to hon. members that wheat can be shipped cheaper via Panama than through the eastern ports. I believe the railroads would find it to their advantage to give more encouragement to the use of Pacific coast ports. In my view the system of our freight tolls is antiquated; that statement was made many years ago before we had truck and other competition. The whole system should be revamped by a practical commission with a view to encouraging the service and to the selling of more railway service to the community. The commission should have in mind, too, the possibility of offsetting truck competition, because, as I have pointed out, if the railways do not go out to meet truck competition their revenues will become smaller and smaller as the years go by. Will the railways and the government stand by and watch the competition grow, a competition which in the end will leave very little freight traffic for our railways?
Since 1920 four changes have been made in the export rates to British Columbia. No change has been made in the domestic rates.
Except in regard to feed grains.

Yes, except in regard to feed grains, but only temporary. Now that the minister has mentioned feed grains I should like to point out something which happened last year and which I believe will serve to indicate the arbitrary attitude taken by the railway companies. Tariff 145 designated certain grades of wheat which would be carried at a rate of 30J cents per 100 pounds. Mill feeds were left out, and they should not have been left out. There is in Cloverdale a cooperative association composed of farmers, an association which buys as cheaply as it can and returns profits to its members. That association bought t,wo carloads of burnt wheat unfit for human consumption. When it was brought to Cloverdale it was distributed among the members of the association, and the numbers 5 and 6 feed rates were charged. About a month later the railway company sent in a bill for $112 per carload indicating that burnt wheat was not under the tariff. It is true that burnt wheat might not have been mentioned under the feed grain tariff, but hon. members will realize that it could be used for no purpose other than that of feeding stock. As a matter of fact it is not very palatable even to poultry, but poultiy-men will buy it because it is a little cheaper. I have mentioned these facts so that the

Railway Act-Rates on Orain

minister may know the attitude of the railway companies, may realize how arbitrary- or shall I use the word unreasonable-they can be at times. Surely they must know that burnt wheat is only feed wheat, and could be used for no other purposes. Whether or not they have changed the rate by this time I am not sure.
On the order paper we have legislation to deal with minimum wages. It is all very well to have a minimum wage rate, so that the workmen will be operating on a better basis, but so long as the province of British Columbia is subjected to these inequalities, in the matter of freight rates, so long as it is being soaked, shall I say, more than the other provinces, the wage changes will not be of very great benefit to that province. What reason can there be for charging a certain rate on a certain article going in one direction and another rate for the same article going in the opposite direction? I know the railway companies can give excuses; they are very good at that. It is marvellous to behold the manner in which they can quibble, as any of us who have had occasion to combat them could testify.
During the hearing of the appeal-and I ask the minister to take special note of this- the commission were asked why the rate was so low from Fort William to the eastern ports, and the reply was that the rate was low because of water competition. The rates for domestic purposes were kept low so 'as to endeavour to capture the trade. However when I asked them how it was that .they had i rate of 25 cents per 100 pounds for domestic purposes as against an export rate of 34J cents irom Fort William to Montreal, they had no answer to make. They had been arguing that the export rate had to be lower so as to induce traffic, and that the domestic rate was considerably higher. Here was an instance however where they had lowered the domestic rate to 25 cents per 100 pounds while the export rate remained at 34i cents. As I pointed out, a man oould very well buy a carload of feed presumably for domestic purposes at 25 cents per 100 pounds, and ship it at the export rate, but if the reverse had been the order, the export rate at 25 cents and the domestic rate at 34J cents, he would not have been allowed to buy the car on the export basis, and use it in the province of British Columbia. No answer was forthcoming in that connection. It is also very interesting to note that the rates were lowered to a considerable degree from Fort William to eastern points due to the fact that the milling companies were beginning to use their own boats. fMr. Reid.]
These interests, which had been encouraged by the railway companies and were given many concessions, were now stepping out, shall I say, to carry their own products on the great lakes. They were the ones who caused the low freight rates which existed on the great lakes last season.
I shall reserve any further observations until other hon. members have spoken. I should like however to repeat this question:	Why
should we in British Columbia be called upon to pay for the heavy losses entailed by the railway companies on steamships, hotels and other investments? I declare the export rate of twenty cents pays. If it does not pay I see no reason why the poeple of British Columbia should be asked to carry the loss. The fact that grain is going through the Pacific ports is to the great advantage of the railways despite the faot that the export rate to Vancouver and New Westminster is a little higher than the rate to the east.	*
This is the fourth time I have introduced this subject. It is not a political matter, but it is one which affects the whole of the province of British Columbia. We are not jealous of the maritime provinces, we wish them the best of luck, but when one notices in the estimates for the present year a vote of almost a million dollars for concessions to the maritime provinces in the matter of freight rates one wonders just how long we in British Columbia will have to cry before we get justice. That is all we are asking. We are not asking for a rate lower than that enjoyed by other provinces; we are not asking for anything unfair; we are asking only for treatment equal to that enjoyed by the eastern and prairie provinces. I would ask the minister, therefore, to take what I have said into serious consideration, and I should be particularly pleased if this year he would allow the second reading to pass and let us go into committee on the bill. I have pointed out repeatedly that it is useless for us in British Columbia to appeal to the board of railway commissioners, and I cannot make that statement too emphatically. That is the actual record. They themselves have quoted case after case, dating from 1917, and they have taken an attitude against any change in past judgments; they have said, "These judgments have been rendered against you, we are very sorry that we can do nothing for you in the matter." So long as these judgments remain and so long as this is the attitude of the board, then I contend that it is useless for us to make any appeal to them. I submit that parliament is the place where the injustice should be righted; it

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
could be righted by this bill and changing the act, and we should then have what the east has enjoyed for many years.
I would ask the minister this question. Why is it that in the Railway Act the words grain and flour cover all grain and grain products, whereas when it comes to shipments to the Pacific coast the railway companies distinguish between export grain and domestic grain? I think the word "grain" should be applicable throughout the dominion. It is our view that this phase of the matter should be looked into.
I am not going to discuss the question of the losses sustained by the railways, nor shall I consider the question whether this is the proper time to make the change. In 1925 the railway companies used the argument then and said that they could not make any change because it would mean a dead loss to them if they did so; they opposed any changes in the export grain rates. Well, the Panama canal and the ports of Vancouver and New Westminster have opened up since. The rates were changed with respect to export in 1925, and what happened? The grain traffic has grown considerably. I submit that if we are looking for markets and for a more equitable adjustment as between different products in the country then one of the first things that should be done is to see that grain products are carried equally mile for mile under similar conditions throughout the dominion. I appeal to the government.

I congratulate my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) on the gallant fight he has put up in connection with the equalization of freight rates in the west, and I support him most heartily. I am not going into the details of this matter; I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house. The hon. member has set forth the arguments and given the details. We know why the rates have not been equalized. I am not prejudiced against any of the railways, but the fact is that in consequence of the mistake made by one of the railways-it is not necessary to be more specific than that-we cannot get an equalization of freight rates to-day. There is a very simple remedy available; there are thousands of railway men in Canada who could tell you what should be done. This afternoon I heard a good deal about a proposed economic council, and the chances are that when the council is established one of the very first things it will submit to this government, or whatever government is in
power, is that the heavy hauls should be over the Yellowhead pass. It seems to me that an arrangement should be made whereby the Canadian Pacific instead of hauling heavy freights up and down the hills, should go through Yellowhead pass, where there is a decent grade. If that were done millions could be saved in transportation in that direction alone. We do not need to go to an economic council for that information; ask any railway man, whether Canadian Pacific or Canadian National, and he will tell you. that.
I cannot understand why not only the members from British Columbia but hon. members on all sides of the house from Alberta to Saskatchewan should not support my hon. friend in the appeal he has made, and I say that for this reason. They have feed grain to sell, and our climatic conditions are favourable to feeding not only poultry but stock. Give us an equalization in freight rates, give us a reduction in the domestic rates, and then the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan will have a market for their feed grain, which they require to-day.
That is all I have to say. I congratulate the hon. member on the fight he has put up, and it is not a political fight. He lives in the Fraser valley where he can see the conditions, and I can appreciate them too although I do not live there. I hope that other hon. members from the west will lay aside their prejudices and assist us, to see whether we cannot obtain a reduction in domestic rates.

I
do not intend to discuss this question at any great length to-night. It has been a live subject and a very important one in British Columbia for many years. Let me say to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Munn) that the members on this side from British Columbia advocated the lowering of the freight rates long before he ever entered this house, and there is not one hon. member from British Columbia to-day who is not in favour of it to-day.

I have listened to the hon.
member several times and have not heard him advocate it.

The hon. gentleman has
not been here long enough.

I have been here long enough to know that.
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

Let the hon. gentleman
read Hansard. This is my tenth year in the house, and I do not believe there is a member from British Columbia who has not supported it during that period. One of the first members from British Columbia to take up this fight on behalf of British Columbia, which was the basis of the contention before the board of railway commissioners, was the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). When a special attorney was sent here by the Oliver government of British Columbia to fight the freight rates, that hon. member was the man who handed over his file and all the information he had, together with a promise of assistance on behalf of British Columbia. And we have followed in close cooperation with him. The only objection I have made has been to the method of obtaining the reduction. I would refer my hon. friend opposite to some of the statements made by his friends in 1925, statements by his own leader and by the former Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler). If my hon. friends will refer to Hansard they will find that both these hon. gentlemen at that time said that the proper body to deal with freight rates was the board of railway commissioners. The former Minister of National Revenue went further and said that if we could not get justice from the board then it was up to us to change the board. I agree with some of the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster in regard to the commission. I will not say that they have not dealt fairly with this matter, but I suggest that they are not a sufficiently judicial body, and I believe that many of these questions might better be taken before two or three judges of the exchequer court. If some arrangement could be made whereby, instead of appealing to this body, we could appeal to such judges to decide the case, I think the results would be more satisfactory. The question must be decided. Are we to undertake, in this house, the adjustment of the freight structure of this great country- a tremendous undertaking. I agree that the time has arrived when some adjustments must be made. During the last ten years great changes have taken place in our transportation systems, and I think it would be in the interest of the railway companies as well as the people to have a full inquiry. To carry traffic at a lower rate might get back some of the business the railways have lost to the truck lines.
As I said before, I do not intend to make a speech on this matter. I am sure that there is not a member on this side, either from
(Mr. Munn.l
British Columbia	or	from any	part ofthe west, who is not in favour of the principle of lower freight rates. I had not the privilege of appearing personally before the tribunal which heard	the	appeal	in thismatter, but before leaving for the west I did appear and left with them a written argument asking for the inclusion of mill feeds in the reduction in rates on feed grains. Mill feeds are necessary to the dairymen of the Fraser valley,	as they	must have bran,shorts and chop.	I	can	assure	the hon.
gentleman that for a number of years we have advocated lower freight rates to British Columbia and we still feel that it is necessary in the interests of the stockmen of that province that a reduction should be made. As to whether or not this reduction should be down to that of the export rate, is a question which will have to be decided but at any rate there should be a reduction on mill feeds to equal that given on feed grains. With these few remarks I hope I have cleared up the suggestion made by the last speaker that we, on this side of the house are opposed to a reduction in the domestic rates on grain. We are for a drastic reduction.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who
introduced this bill (Mr. Reid) stated that he wished to reply, so I should like to know if he intends to allow this bill to go to a vote to-night. If that is his intention I can finish my remarks at one minute to nine o'clock, but if he desires to make a reply, I shall have to go into the question more fully.

I said that I would like to
leave the remainder of my remarks until later. I was reserving that part of my statement in case the government turned down the bill. If the government is going to do that then I feel it incumbent upon me to reply to the minister.

The hon. gentleman will
have to reply because the government cannot accept this bill. It is obvious to anyone who gives much thought to the matter that the government could not accept this measure. Hon. gentlemen opposite are boasting that they expect to have their party in power after the next election-

No question about
that.

I think that is a futile
boast. Let me say to them that in supporting a bill of this sort they are laying up trouble for themselves if they should be so fortunate as to come back to power after the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
next election. Any government, whether this one or any other, that attempts to make freight rates in this parliament will be occupied with nothing else but the making of those rates. Members from all sections of Canada will be presenting bills and we will have in this parliament a log rolling contest of the most exceptional kind. Hon. members from Quebec, from certain portions of Ontario, from New Brunswick and British Columbia will be wanting special rates on pulpwood. Hon. members from the prairie provinces will be asking for special rates on their grain products, and hon. members from the hay raising sections of Canada will be asking for special rates on that commodity. It is obvious that parliament cannot undertake to fix freight rates for the Dominion of Canada. In 1904 the board of railway commissioners was set up for the purpose of dealing with freight rates. Whether that board is a perfectly functioning body to-day is another question. Without wishing to reflect upon it in any way, I do not say that it is, but that is a different question. The matter of the reformation of the board of railway commissioners is an altogether different question from that of this parliament deciding to make freight rates. The opportunity to appeal from the ruling of the board has always been open to anyone. At the present time my hon. friend is appealing from a ruling on this question and that appeal will come up in due time before the present government. In spite of the fact that this privilege has been open to all during the years, no government has changed or altered a judgment of the board. At certain times different governments have referred back certain questions to the board and asked that they be reconsidered.
The parliament of Canada has not the proper machinery to deal with this most complicated of questions, so parliament has always taken the attitude that it cannot make freight rates. The hon. gentleman, in what has been a fair speech in a general way, has to-night asked this house, the members of which are not familiar with freight rates, to pass upon the judgment of the board of railway commissioners.

speechtext:
When this item was up on
Thursday evening last, the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) suggested that the item should stand in view of what might be contained in the report of the price spreads commission. As it is apparent that that report will not be down for some time it is felt that the item should not stand any longer. On the same occasion the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) made some reference to car loadings of coal m the prairie provinces, and as a result of his observations and interrogation, a statement has been prepared by the weights and measures branch with regard to that particular matter. This statement ;I desire to present to the committee.
In the matter of discrepancies in the weight of coal shipped in cargo lots from the Alberta mines, it is suggested that this is essentially ft railway matter and will be taken up with the railway commission. As a matter of fact this trouble has been ghen a good deal of attention by the weights and measures service. As a result of complaints in 1924, the weights and measures inspectors in Calgary and Edmonton were instructed to arrange with the railway officials to check-weigh a number of empty freight cars in the coal service, and from this check it was shown that the root of the trouble lay in the inaccuracy of stencilled tare weights, caused by repairing and strengthening cars, by refuse, including coal dust left in the cars, and by rain, snow and ice. The results of these tare weighings were sent to the railway commission in 1925 and 1926 for their information and action, and these checks were made arnually for a number of years as the only thing the weights and measures branch could do to try to improve the situation. The work proved effective, for in March, 1930, out of sixty-one cars checked at Edmonton and Drumheller, all but two cars showed errors of only three hundred pounds and less, which the railways consider correct, and since then the department has not received a single complaint.
The officers also check-weighed a number of loaded cars and asked consignee to return unloading weights, and on eight shipments only relatively small errors were reported, only two being over five hundred pounds. In two cases there were errors of 1,250 pounds and 5,330 pounds on two 30-ton cars, and this error was definitely traced to inaccuracy on the part of consignee in unloading in small lots, a factor that should not be overlooked and one which would not be corrected by net loading. This demonstrated that if reasonable care were taken, freight car loading and weighing would give reasonably

The inspectors at Edmonton and Calgary are again being instructed to arrange with the railways to make another check-weighing of empty cars at the Edmonton and Drumiheller mines, and as soon as these results are obtained, the matter will again be taken up with the railway commission. The railway scales are not in question. They are inspected yearly by the weights and measures inspectors by means of a 60,000-pound test car.

speakeroldname: Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The policy of the government with regard to the Department of National Defence is identical, so far as I know, with the policies adopted by governments in the past. There should be a department to take charge of the defence of the country. There should be a force, represented by the three branches of the service, capable of undertaking the defence of the country should the country's boundaries be in jeopardy. That force is divided into the naval service, the militia service and the air service and it is composed of the permanent and non-permanent forces. The permanent force is a small, highly trained, extremely efficient body of officers and men which in times of peace largely acts as a training force for the non-permanent active militia. The non-permanent active militia is composed of the various branches of the militia service, the air service and the naval service, and it is an entirely voluntary body of men whose payment by the country is simply that payment which reaches them for the period of training each year. They go out for their training and the recompense which they receive is but small. The expenses, therefore, to which those non-permanent units are put are very largely paid by the officers of those units, to whom in my opinion the country owes a considerable debt of gratitude. They give their time, their interest and their service, and we have but to look back to the outbreak of war in 1914 to see the test to which the defence forces of Canada were put. The plans which had been made, somewhat modified year by year, were put into operation and these skeleton forces were rapidly expanded into such bodies of men as were capable of joining the contingents of other parts of the empire in the war into which unfortunately we were cast, for the protection and security of the country.
I do not know that in any way the Department of National Defence has changed what has been the policy of the department in this country for many years past. It has to see to it that the forces at its disposal are kept up to the mark; that at .least an attempt is made to keep abreast of modern developments in the conduct of punitive expeditions, and it has to maintain a service of efficiency

which will stand the test when the testing time comes. In addition it fulfils another duty, that the force should be distributed throughout Canada in the military districts in such a way that if called upon by the provincial governments in times of stress and strain, through civil disturbances within their own boundaries, they can render such assistance as may be necessary to support the police forces of the country. The Department of National Defence, therefore, is retained and upheld for these twTo main purposes.

I am pleased to hear the discussion which has taken place on this item. The remarks I should like to make may have some bearing on following items in the estimates, but perhaps it would be convenient to complete my observations at this time. During the last few days I believe that as citizens we have been compelled to give more serious consideration than has been given in the last twelve or fifteen years to the estimates of the Department of National Defence. Hon. members should consider these votes and ask themselves what we have reserved for the $9,000,000 or $12,000,000 or such sums as have been voted in the years following the close of the last war. The vote has increased from $8,000,000 to $10,000,000, $11,000,000 and so on. II believe it is quite in order that hon. members should ask what we are getting for these large sums of money, and whether we are getting what we should have at the present time.
Some time ago I spoke about the nature and the extent of the next war. The result has been that there has been an increase in the estimates along the lines I suggested. We note an increase in the estimates for the air force, amounting to about $700,000. Undoubtedly history has shown that we have always been preparing for the past war, not for the future war. Following the continental wars and the wars of the American independence we put all our time and consideration upon improving the infantry. Following the South African war we directed our energies to an improvement of the cavalry and the mounted infantry. Since the close of the great war it may be that we have been going a little too far in the development of artillery. In other words we are constantly prepai-ing for the war that is past, not for the war that is likely to come.
If I had my way there would be no more wars. I have had as much experience in war as any hon. member of the house. Possibly more. The old British army without a doubt has outlived its day and has gone. What a

Supply-National Defence
splendid history it had! Beginning under adverse opinion it worked its way into the_ affections of the people, the parliament and even its enemies. When the army of Marlborough returned from its great wars and victories the imen were treated as plagues. In England they were looked upon as pests, despite the fact that they had only recently returned from their glorious victories. Following 1763, when through the acquisition of colonies Great Britain became an empire, the suggestion was made that theTe be a standing army to be used to garrison the outposts of the empire. The people in parliament treated that army as another plague, and the cry of ""down with the standing army" was raised. Mercenaries had to be hired to do the work, and the service given was altogether unsatisfactory. Again in 1815 the British army returned home after its glorious victories, having saved the empire and perhaps the whole of civilization. Again they were treated as plagues and pests. After 1815, however, the empire was greatly enlarged by acquisitions of considerable extent, and accordingly a force had to be raised and maintained. What treatment did it receive? Instead of being retained at home practically the whole army was banished to foreign service and had to undergo great misery and suffering. In Australia it lived in a state of wretchedness. In Cape Colony, now Cape Province, it was almost abandoned; in the tropical countries yellow fever almost wiped them out, eighty per cent of the force vanishing each year. In the West Indies, where we are told there is a delightful climate, the army lost forty per cent of its number. In Minorca the army was sent without bedding and meat was omitted from the ration. In Burma in 182426 it marched through the jungles without vegetables, milk or meat and only one out of seven of that army returned. I am giving this historical illustration to show what the army has gone through and what splendid service it has rendered to the empire. Here was an army in terrible condition, passing through cruel suffering in the Crimea, and for the first time the British public began to realize its responsibilities. For the first time [DOT] the people of Great Britain began to see that they were responsible for that army and for the conditions under which they served, and for the first time British soldiers returned from victory to be decently treated by the British people and the British parliament. The army has had a wonderful history, and I bring this up because I want the house to realize how much the
empire has owed to the army in the past, what splendid service it has given and what a record it has -made for the British people. British soldiers entered a country on every occasion as an enemy, and invariably oame out friends of the people into whose country they went. In South Africa the British army marched through the whole field without one complaint from the citizens of misbehaviour. The Peninsular army marched from the Pyrenees up to the channel and returned home without a complaint from a single citizen.
This is the army we have been proud of, but its day is gone. It has left a great responsibility, however, upon the people of the British empire, upon the people of Canada, that of seeing that similar conditions do not prevail in the future. If another war should come, which God forbid, let us see to it that those who go first shall not be left in the position of those who went first in former wars. One hundred thousand were completely wiped out for lack of preparedness; one hundred thousand lives were practically sacrificed in order to afford time to make preparations so as to meet the enemy. Consider what we are doing. What I am about to say is not intended as criticism, though perhaps we have been indifferent. The old army is gone. We have remnants of it going around yet; we have an infantry parading with rifles, which are as obsolete to-day as the bow and arrow when you remember that there are machine guns. We have the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery in Kingston without horses; and yet they include swords and spurs in their equipment. If you want to realize what is really important so far as service goes I would ask you to read a part of the report of the Department of National Defence. Let us read that report and ask ourselves whether we are satisfied with the conditions which that report discloses. There is no question whatever that the air will be of greatest importance in future preparations. I would refer the committee to page 76 of the report for this year, though there may be some changes, and I would ask the minister whether in his opinion an increase of $700,000 is sufficient for preparations. If the minister says that he is satisfied with what this report discloses then I do not think that this house should be satisfied. If we are to have an air force, and it is one of the three I consider necessary, then it should be properly equipped, and it is the duty of the members of this house and of the citizens of this country to see that the force is properly equipped. No doubt the minister will discuss this matter, and I am sure he will agree with me that the present state of affairs is not satisfactory. I want him to tell me whether he really thinks that an increase of $700,000 is adequate. Every member of this house and every citizen in the country, I have not the slightest doubt, will advise him to get after the air force and introduce modern types-that is, if we are to have a defence force as more than something to play with, if it is at all necessary, and if this vote of $9,000,000 is not to be lightly passed over without proper consideration. It may be, with these dark and threatening clouds overhead, that we may change our whole equipment and our whole policy, and on this point I will speak later.
Leaving the air force for the present, let us see what the situation is so far as the sea is concerned. Again we have nothing but the splendid recollection of the wonderful British fleet. How these names have stirred us from boyhood up, the names of great sailors who have made the British empire what it is. But the battleships of the earlier days are gone; their usefulness has ceased. Speeds of twenty and twenty-one knots an hom- are no longer adequate; to-day they are building the nine and ten thousand ton cruiser with a speed of thirty and thirty-one knots. But after all, is that the important part of the defence

force? I am sure that the hon. gentleman is sincere, but just think of the great Pacific coast absolutely without any defence. We have two or three little cruisers there, and as soon as any trouble arises you will have to bring them in behind a rock or under cover somewhere. If trouble arose between any other two nations this country would suffer. What is practical sea defence to-day? It is no longer battleships or cruisers, it is the submarine. The history of the last war shows the important part played by submarines. I hope the committee will grant me a few moments to give a picture of what happened during the last war.
In August, 1914, we lost 40,200 tons of shipping through the action of submarines. In July, 1917, we lost 364,000 tons by this means. During the period of the war 6,692,000 tons of British shipping were sent to the bottom and at the beginning of the war we had only 20,000,000 tons. We were finally losing more ships than it was possible to replace under any policy of shipbuilding. If we are going to have naval defence, the only defence I can see will be of any use to us is that furnished by submarines. The cost of this type of defence is very small when compared with the cost of training infantry, cavalry and so on. Lloyd's estimate that during the war we lost 5,861 vessels with a tonnage of something like 13,233,172, a figure greater than the one I have given.
I do not wish to detain the committee, but there is a point or two I should like to bring to its attention. If we are to have defence, I think we should spend the money on something which will be up to date and let the rest go. I should like to make two or three proposals. I suggest that the future policy of defence should not be left in the hands of the three or four permanent officers who compose the council. No one knows whether they ever meet and no one knows what propositions are considered. I think this council should include some public representation. The future war will not be a matter of bullets and powder, it will be a matter of industrial activity.

That is industry. We have heard a lot about councils to-day, but I think the one spoken of this afternoon is going to work out. I believe civilian representation on the defence council would be of great assistance.
There is another objectionable matter in connection with the permanent forces. These forces are made up of a number of young men and in my opinion they should be en-

eouraged to make permanent homes. Yet when they want to get married they are told that they must wait their turn. A man may have to wait about fifteen years in order to get a place. I say to this council that they should cut out the swords and the spurs, eliminate these antiquities and let the men of the permanent forces marry when they will and give them an extra allowance when they do marry. If this is done I think we will have a better force, as the men will appreciate this.
Men have been permitted to rise in the permanent forces step by step and retire when they have reached the limit of superannuation or pension to enter into competition with other people in civil government appointments. There are men with thousands of dollars of pension occupying civil government positions paying salaries of eight, nine or ten thousand dollars. The same thing happens with great war pensions. Men are receiving pensions of $180 a month and occupying other government positions. This thing should be evened up. When a man has a substantial pension I think he should be satisfied and not try to occupy another position.
I should like to refer to another matter in connection with the forces in the north. These men are out of contact with their families. A short time ago a young man from my constituency who was in the signal corps alone on Camsell river disappeared, it being supposed that he was drowned. He had a life insurance policy amounting to $2,000, by which $1,000 was left to his mother and $1,000 to his father. In addition he had about $200 in the bank. It has taken every cent of the money he had in the bank as well as some of the insurance money to get his estate settled up. The department insisted that the insurance policies should be sent up north in order that his estate might be settled. I am mentioning this simply as something which may concern other boys who are in the north in the flying or signal corps. This boy was an only son and the parents have been put to considerable expense in having his estate settled. I hope the minister will see that in future cases the department will be fair.

Mr. Chairman, (I
should like to go back to the point I was discussing just before the hon. member for Kingston Oity (Mr. Ross) rose. I quite agree with the hon. member that spurs, swords and that sort of thing are obsolete, and that undoubtedly from the standpoint of defence the air forces are the ones that will be used most in any coming war. But
it seems to me that war itself is or ought to be obsolete; that arms have been shown to be no real defence and that we are to-day simply playing with this whole business. I am not so much concerned about the expenditure of the $15,000,000, although that is a large amount and it might very well be used to much better advantage, but I believe this expenditure of $15,000,000 not only is very largely a waste of money but so far as other nations are concerned, tends to be provocative and at the same time to lull us into a sense of false security. We have undoubtedly come to a position in the history of the world when no one nation can stand alone and hope to defend itself against all comers; yet that is practically the position which the Minister of National Defence is taking, that in a vague sort of way we have to have the army, the navy and the air forces to be able to defend ourselves effectively. That is an altogether fallacious way of looking at the matter; it belongs to an earlier age and not to the situation in which we find ourselves to-day.
We have had references again and again to the strength of the British navy. That may have been all very well in the old days, but I would point out that that strength is not what it once was. At one time Great Britain thought she ought to be able to have a naval strength equal to that of any other two countries. Those claims have had to be surrendered. More recently she thought she ought to be equal in naval power to the United States, to any one other naval power. Those claims too can hardly be maintained. It is only within the last few months that the old idea of the ratio of five, five, three, as between England, the United States and Japan, has been challenged, and with the disarmament conference practically dissolved, we do not know what may happen in the future.
I spoke a few minutes ago about the Pacific. Anyone who knows anything at all about the strength of the Japanese navy must recognize that if anything happened in the orient-and the Japanese may easily break out at any time-our western coast would be exposed to one of the greatest navies of the world, and I do not think anyone can say that Canada alone would be equal to defending herself. Then it is not at all clear that in such a contingency we could rely upon the British navy. That is why I ask whether any arrangements are being made by which we could have cooperation with the United States navy; for I would point out, as is recognized even by many of the British authorities to-day, that

Canada's interests on the North American continent are essentially different from those of Great 'Britain, and as one of the Pacific powers we shall have to deal with the situation on the Pacific. I think we have a very considerable advantage in being a neighbour to a great nation, the United States; yet I would be one of the last to suggest that we should come to depend upon them and be gradually absorbed into the great United States republic. But let us look at the situation: if trouble broke out between Japan and either the United States or Canada, these two nations would be drawn in together; that is a real situation to-day.
There was a day when we felt we were simply colonials and could more or less depend upon Great Britain and would have to follow her lead. With all due respect to the United Kingdom, I think most of the people of this country think of Canada, as an independent nation within the boundaries of the commonwealth of British nations, but do we propose simply to follow the British lead? We have really no voice in the determination of the war or peace policies of Great Britain. She may become involved in Africa, India, the far east, and then without our having had any participation in the perliminary arrangements, we may be asked to assist. Canada did assist in a military way back in 1014, but personally I am of opinion that it would not be so easy now as it was in 1914 to rally the Canadian people to send troops to Europe, and that not through any disloyalty to the British empire, but because a new idea has come to our people as it has to a great many of the peoples of the world. I would say this, that one of these days unless we throw ourselves into some sort of imperial conference in which we shall have a real participation and can have a real voice-and this few would advocate-we shall be faced with a situation where we may be called upon once again to back Great Britain and we may refuse to do so. Great Britain will, without our having had any participation, present us with a fait accompli. Then what? Can we depend upon the sentiment of the Canadian people? Personally I do not think so, and under such circumstances it would be only fair for us now to say frankly to Great Britain: We do not propose at any time to throw ourselves into a European war. I believe that would be the sentiment of two-thirds of the Canadian people to-day. Surely it would be fairer for us to intimate that to Great Britain at this time than to wait until she is in a tight pinch and then fall back and refuse to give her help. Those are con-

siderations that should be fairly laid before our people and definitely decided upon.
When the great- war was over, I take it that the vast number of people had come to the conclusion that war was a failure; that war settled nothing Whatever. War was waged against Germany, war has given us in place of the kaiser, a Hitler, and in place of the bureaucracy the Nazis-no very great improvement. War did not settle the affairs of Europe; European affairs are in as great a turmoil to-day as they were prior to the w'ar of 1914. There are imminent dangers both on the continent of Europe and in the far east. War has settled nothing. The warring nations after the armistice got together and decided that they would try to secure peace through some other means than armaments. Then came the treaty of Versailles and the setting up of the League of Nations. Well, the last few days have I presume disillusioned a great many people with regard to the security to be obtained through the League of Nations. We have seen the German nation through Hitler absolutely repudiate the Versailles treaty, and of course we are all indignant over that. But let me point out that Germany is correct in her contention that she was not the first to repudiate the Versailles treaty, that the allies failed to live up to their obligations under it. When Germany laid down her arms, she laid them down on the express condition that the other nations would proceed to disarm. That the allies have not done. We might as well frankly face this situation. Hitler may be as bad as most of us think him, but at the same time we must admit that the development of feeling that has taken place in Germany in the last few years is quite understandable on account of the treatment we have accorded her. I do not want to go into that question in any great detail, but lest anyone should think I am expressing merely a . personal opinion, I picked up from my file an article written by Lloyd George and appearing in our papers of 'September 10, 1932. In this article he has this to say:
There were four men primarily responsible for framing the treaty of Versailles, which terminated the greatest war in human history. M. Clemenceau, President Wilson, Signor Orlando and myself.
It not only recast national boundaries in two continents, but it sought to inaugurate a new reign of peaceful adjustment in international disputes by substituting machinery of justice for mechanism of force.
That was the purpose, an effort to substitute the machinery of justice for the mechanism of force. I submit that in the estimates which are before the committee to-day we are still clinging to the idea of the

Supply-National Defence
mechanism of force. Nearly every nation is doing the same, although we did dream for a little while of substituting the machinery of justice. He goes on:
To carry out this idea practically, we imposed upon Germany, who was accused of trampling by organized violence on international right, the most ruthless destruction of its peccant armaments.
When the German delegates displayed' natural hesitation about accepting these conditions, which reduced their fatherland to impotence in an armed world, Clemenceau wrote them a letter on behalf and at the request of his colleagues, assuring the Germans that their disarmament would be treated as a prelude to steps for general reduction of armaments by the other nations.
This pledge is also expressed in the covenant of the League of Nations. It was accepted by all the signatories of the treaty and ratified by their senates.
Two out of four who drafted that solemn undertaking have passed away, Clemenceau and Wilson. Signor Orlando and I remain.
Now I ask the committee to listen to this:
As one of the two survivors, I have no hesitation in accepting the German view that the victorious nations have shamelessly broken faith on the question of armaments. I should be surprised to hear that my co-survivor, Orlando, took a different view of the turpitude of the victors in this respect.
That is strong language, but it is the language of one who knew the situation, and it is substantiated by the text of the treaty itself. He said:
I have no hesitation in accepting the German view that the victorious nations have shamelessly broken faith on the question of armaments.
Then he went on:
, The Germans revolt against unscrupulous agitators and designing militarists. Statesmen of the fatherland' have for thirteen years shown a degree of patience, forbearance and restraint which is worthy of the great people they represented. Throughout this period the bond they entered in an hour of crushing defeat was being enforced relentlessly against Germany and her allies, whilst other parties to the contract insolently refused even to discuss performance of their part of the agreement.
Under the circumstances I do not think that we can altogether blame Germany for the action which she has taken, lamentable as we feel that it is. But that simply opens up the whole question of what we are going to do about it. Comparatively few of our Canadian people have taken the Versailles treaty very seriously. Within the last few weeks the present government have been introducing considerable legislation on the ground that it was obligatory on us to implement pledges which we made at the time of the signing of
the peace treaty. Notwithstanding that, we have not taken the league seriously. We have been members, it is true, but we hardly ever discuss in this house what the league is doing; in fact the tendency has been more or less to scoff at the league. I confess that for a long time I for one had no use at all for the league. To me it was largely a league of victors, and it was only after other nations, such as Germany, began to come in that it seemed to me that possibly it might be used as an instrument for bringing about peace. To-day I am not so sure whether under the present leadership, and under the present system, we can depend upon the league. In any case I submit that we in Canada have not carried out our obligations as members of the league. For example, article 10 says:
The members of the league undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing independence of all members of the league. In ease of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression the council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
Or again, article 16:
Should any member of the league resort to war in disregard of its covenants under articles 12, 13 or 15, it shall ipso facto be deemed to have committed an act of war against all other members oif the league, which hereby undertake immediately to subject it to the severance of all trade or financial relations, the prohibition of all intercourse between their nationals and the nationals of the covenantbreaking state, and the prevention of all financial, commercial or personal intercourse between the nationals of the covenant-breaking state and the nationals of any other state, whether a member of the league or not. . . .
The members of the league agree, further, that they will mutually support one another in the financial and economic measures which are taken under this article, in order to minimize the loss and inconvenience resulting from the above measures, and that they will mutually support one another in resisting any special measures aimed at one of their number by the covenant-breaking state ...
These are some very clear cut pledges that we, together with the other signatories, gave at the time of the signing of the peace treaty. We had the matter tested in the case of the incident in Manchuria when Japan, although not formally declaring war, practically engaged in war against China and took part of what was generally recognized as Chinese territory. What did we do? Our representatives rather meekly followed the lead of Sir John Simon in the matter and refused to live up to our obligations, with the result that Japan ultimately took over Manchuria, set up her own puppet state there and to-day is launching still further attacks upon China that seriously

menace the peace of the far east. We have not lived up to our obligations under this treaty.
Now I come to the question of the purpose of our army. I asked the Minister of National Defence to-day how far we are prepared for effective action. He said not a word as to our obligations under these clauses of the treaty, not a word. If we are in any sense depending upon securing peace through the league, then it seems to me the only thing we as a member of the league can do is to live up to our obligations. Surely that is a reasonable position to take. But we have persistently refused to surrender any of our narrow self-interest. We have refused to surrender our sovereignty -and not we alone but nearly all the nations of the world-notwithstanding that all history shows that smaller units have had to give place to larger organizations, and that to-day no nation can live into itself.
I must confess I often feel, as I know a great many of my fellow Canadians do, that we must more or less retire into ourselves and escape from entangling alliances with Europe. But suppose we do try to live to ourselves; have we solved our problem? I come back to this question: Are we in Canada to-day prepared to throw ourselves into an adequate national defence scheme? If we alone, without reliance upon the British empire or upon the members of the league of which we form a part, propose to defend ourselves against all comers, then it is surely obvious that our defence is hopelessly inadequate. Instead of spending $15,000,000 I suppose we ought to pour out the money, but I do not think we would be any better off then than we are to-day. Are we going to depend upon Great Britain? If we are I am QOt so sure that logically the advocates of a contribution to the British navy have not a good deal to say for themselves. If we are going to depend upon that navy it might be well said that we should contribute to it. I say this might be the logical position to take, though personally I cannot believe that our salvation will come about through depending upon the British navy or making a contribution to it.
Are we going to depend upon the United States? I fancy that in case of an outbreak say between Japan and the United States, Canada would be dragged in and it might very well be that the United States would be glad to defend us against aggression. Then is our destiny to be absorbed by the United States? Some of my ancestors came to Canada after the revolutionary war in order to

be on British territory, and I cannot very well contemplate political absorption by the United States, much as I should like to see a very much closer economic connection than we have to-day. But are we going to depend upon the United States? Is there nothing ahead but international anarchy?
When I brought up this matter a year ago it was the acting Minister of Immigration, if I remember rightly, who rather rebuked me. He decried this talk about war, but there has been war in the past and I submit that if the predisposing causes remain there will be war in the future, and we cannot very well read the dispatches of the last few days without recognizing that war in the not remote future is not an improbable thjng. Most Canadians want peace. When I brought up this matter the other night the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) delivered a regular tirade against me, and spoke as though I had been lecturing the house. Nothing was further from my thoughts. I am not intending to do that now. The Minister of Railways spoke as though we could take it for granted that we all wanted peace. I think most of us do want peace; I think most hon. members opposite and most of the Liberals want peace, just as we in this corner and most of the citizens of Canada want peace. There is an occasional man, however, who seems to hanker after war. About a year ago I noticed in the press that Colonel Cock-shutt had this to say:
These have been rather dark days for soldiers, but the glorious days will come again. . . . Europe to-day is in a turmoil, and Canada's men of war may yet be needed. The spirit of the empire still lives.
I hope that is not characteristic of the attitude of a majority of Canadians, but I do urge that we are not going to get peace simply by wishing for it or praying for it; we will get world peace only as we definitely adopt those measures which will bring about peace. By relying upon the expenditure of $15,000,000 we are only deluding ourselves as to our security.
I think perhaps one thing ought to be fairly well taken for granted, and that is that Canada should not be committed to war except with the consent of the people.
Then we will not need a navy.

I do not think
the people would consent, but I think the hon. member who has just interjected a re-
