mark will agree with the principle that Canada should not be committed to war except with the consent of her people. This does not seem so very radical when we remember that Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, in that rather famous Hamilton speech of October 10, 1927, said:
If ever the time should come when the spectre of 1914 should again appear I believe it would be best, not only that parliament should be called, but that the decision of the government which, of course, would have to be given promptly, should be submitted to the judgment of the people at a general election before troops should leave our shores.
That seems not an unreasonable suggestion; I think that is fairly sound. I know there would be dangers in anything like an election or a plebiscite, but there are dangers whatever way we look. By signing the Kellogg pact, we have renounced war as an instrument of national policy. Am I right in interpreting that to mean that no Canadians should be forced to leave Canada's shores? Possibly most of us would like to take that position, yet a merely negative policy will get us nowhere. I am urging that if we are serious about this matter we must either throw ourselves much more definitely into individual national defence, which I think is hopeless, or else we must more definitely strive to develop the collective system of security. In civil life we have set up our courts and our boards of arbitration. Cannot we do more of that sort of thing in international affairs?
I admit that this problem is very complicated. It is a problem of the ages. People keep asserting that we always have had war and we always will have war. Ah, the wars of the past were comparatively small, local wars-until the last great world war, but I think it is recognized by everyone that any future war must be on a very extensive front and that it will be far more devastating than anything we have known in the past, even the world war. It would seem as though we, as rational beings, should at least attempt some action that would prevent furtheT disaster. Only to-day I received a letter from a French mother in the province of Quebec begging me as an individual to do something to save her children from ever being dragged into another war. She had been reading the papers for the last two or three days, and she asked that something should be done. Surely these appeals by our Canadian people, the fathers and mothers across this country, cannot go unregarded.
I want to emphasize this point, even if I have to repeat it again and again. I do not 92582-119
think that by passing defence estimates, by maintaining the military, naval and air strength that we have to-day, we are doing anything effective to defend this country. I am one of those "impossible idealists," if you like to use that phrase, who believe that by this physical force upon which we have depended in the past we can no longer be sure of defending our people or this country. The world war proved convincingly that war is futile. The other day someone on the other side of the house, I think it was the Minister of Railways, was rather inclined to imply that I was not sympathetic enough to the returned men who fought in the last war.
I did not make any statement of that kind.

I am glad to think the minister did not make that statement, and I quite readily accept his word. I want to state that some of us do admire the heroism of the men who fought in the last war. I have met a great many hundreds, yes thousands of them, and I believe the returned men are among the foremost in stating that they do not want to go to another war. They do not believe that through war we shall obtain permanent peace. Can we not work out the implications of statements of that kind? I have ventured to delay the passage of these estimates for this length of time- Perhaps I should not admit I am delaying their passage-because I believe this matter is of tremendous importance. It seems to me there ought to be a more complete discussion of the whole situation. Perhaps it would be more fitting if such discussion came under the Department of External Affairs, but we cannot separate the two. The Department of External Affairs might be expected to determine our policy, but we must remember that under this vote we have the army through which we would execute a policy that involved military action. For that reason the two departments cannot be separated.
My purpose in opening the discussion has been to call attention to the inadequacy of our present defence, the inadequacy of any military defence under the existing world conditions, and the absolute necessity of taking more seriously our obligations under the league. We must come to realize that it is not sufficient merely to be a member of the league. If we are to have security we must pursue the long and arduous task of gradually developing a certain peace technique ; we must work out constructive policies which may involve the scrapping of many of our old narrow nationalistic and militaristic ideas.

These may have to go, but the future of our country and of our children is at stake. I urge that we do not delude ourselves into thinking that we are safe because we pass an estimate for $15,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), and I listened, too, to his discourse only a few days ago regarding what we should do towards establishing peace not only in Canada but in the rest of the world. To-day he has indicated what we should do to protect ourselves. I do not think any hon. member would expect a vote of money sufficient to protect our great mileage of coast line and the mileage of international boundary between this country and the United States. As the youngest member in His Majesty's loyal opposition in this House of Commons I believe I am speaking for the younger generation in Canada when I say that if Canada is called upon to defend herself she can depend upon the boys and girls of this country to do their utmost in her protection. I do not make that statement boastfully, but rather to express the view that we would in her actual defence be only too proud to emulate the splendid qualities of the young men of 1914-15.
To-night I do not wish to say anything further regarding war and the view taken by the alarmists of the present situation. I sincerely trust that the situation is not nearly so serious as it appears to-day. I have risen to ask a question of the minister regarding one of the most serious wars with which we are now confronted, namely the war against hunger and starvation, a condition with which many people in the Dominion of Canada are faced. Some few nights ago the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) asked the minister to place on Hansard the number of relief camps, by provinces, and the number of men employed in each. Would the minister give that information to the committee?

I was not aware of that, and must thank the minister.

I have listened attentively to the speeches which have been made concerning war. Having served in the last war I believe I may speak with some practical experience. Upon many occasions I have observed that the next war in Europe, so far as we are concerned, must be cash on

delivery. Notwithstanding that fact, however, I believe we must come to earth and view the matter from a realistic standpoint. I am a staunch supporter of the League of Nations; I believe in its development and, if necessary, in the maintenance of an international police force. As Canadians however we must get down to earth and find out where we fit into the world structure. If we may judge from the amount of the expenditure now involved the world has not much to fear from this dominion so far as the development of a warlike spirit is concerned. Our fortunate geographic position places us in a position where we are not called upon to make enormous expenditures for armaments. If we were situated as are New Zealand or Australia, in the cockpit of the next war in the Pacific, quite possibly we would have to take an entirely different attitude in matters of defence. Whether we like it or not Canadians must make up their minds where they fit in, so far as the Pacific question is concerned. We must decide whether we will go along with the Anglo-Saxons and maintain those ideals for which we stand, or whether in the event of war in the Pacific we would remain neutral.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has indicated that we cannot wish ourselves out of the situation. We will have to take a realistic viewpoint, as the Australians have done. The population of Japan, that small island in the Pacific is growing very rapidly, and that country feels it needs an outlet for its surplus population. Should they take it into their heads to cross the Pacific and attempt to settle some of their surplus population in Canada, I should like to feel that we would be secure. I believe the next war may begin something like smallpox; you do not know where it is coming from or when it is going to strike. I should not like it to be said that I am advocating the development of our war services, but I should like to have careful consideration of our position not so much in relation to Europe as in relation to the Pacific. No one has supported more strongly than I have the devolpmemt of the League of Nations as a practical, and driving force towards the1 maintenance of world peace. We must remember however that we cannot divorce ourselves from what is going on around us. As the nation with the fifth greatest trade in the world I believe Canada is most fortunate to be mere or less sitting in the laps of Great Britain and the country to the south of us. Our defences are not at all in conformity with the position we occupy

Supply-National Defence
in world trade. Our good fortune lies in the f.aot first, that we are fortunate in our geographical situation, and second, that we form part of the commonwealth of the British empire.
At the moment the peoplte of Australia are recognizing the gravity of their situation, and I believe we must consider carefully our position. I believe any hon. member who passed through the last war, as I did, would not wish another one, and in that stand I believe they would be supported by the Canadian people. However we must be practical about the matter and take into consideration the attitude of the predominant world forces towards the defence of those institutions which have been developed after much sacrifice.

It is now clear that the treaty of Versailles was an iniquitous treaty, and that war would inevitably result from it unless it were modified. The treaty was based on vengeance. It sought to put the whole blame on one nation though it is now historically admitted that one nation was not wholly to blame. The allies tried to make Germany pay an impossible sum by way of reparations, and then would not receive payment in goods. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has pointed out, they made very definite promises to Germany but did not keep them. That is to say, we the allies smashed the treaty of Versailles all to pieces to suit our purpose, and we cannot very well now suddenly work up a lot of righteous indignation and say that nations which we regarded formerly as our enemies are now showing signs of becoming once more militant. We indeed have sown the wind and almost surely we shall reap the whirlwind. I think the great and ever-increasing cause of war is the bitter competition or struggle for ever diminishing markets. We want to dispose of the weight of goods which each nation is seeking to sell in what are called the markets of the world, though no one knows what that means or where those markets are, and notwithstanding the fact that the people in each country would like to enjoy the goods which they are making such strenuous efforts to sell abroad. In my opinion we have, in the great mass of the unemployed in this country and elsewhere-here it is comparatively small seeing that our population is small-a tinder box. The unemployed have little hope in life, no hope of adventure, no hope of being able to move, no hope of having a variety of food, clothing and entertainment, so that war might seem an interesting thing to them. After all there W582-119i
would be food, clothing and shelter, and some certainty of death at the end. That I know is a terrible statement to make, but I believe there is a good deal of truth in it. Unless the economic problem is solved in each nation or by all the nations cooperating-and in my opinion it will be solved largely by each nation individually-so that the goods which we have in such abundance can be made available to the people of the country, allowing for international trading in those commodities which one nation needs and another wants, then I say that war is inevitable. There are two methods of distributing goods, one is to change the economic system within the country itself, and in my opinion this involves far-reaching monetary changes. The other method is provided by war. If war were declared to-morrow, within forty-eight hours we should be doing the very things which we now say we cannot do; we know very well that the moment war was declared we could move all the goods and services required and we should be able to finanace the moving of those goods and services. To put it in other words, we should then discover that real wealth is the basis of wealth tokens or money. I am apprehensive. I wish I could be as lighthearted about the whole matter as the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Campbell) who seems to think that anyone is an alarmist who talks about war. I do not think he is reading the signs of the times very well if he comes to that conclusion, because the signs are ominous, the real remedy for war lies deep; it lies in justice, economic justice within the nations and between the nations. I believe we could do a lot within our own nation. I agree with someone who said that Canada has not taken her work in the League of Nations very seriously. Once I had the privilege of attending a meeting of the League of Nations and I heard an address iby the Great German, Stressmann, I had to wait for the translation before I could know the words he used, but though I did not know the language he was speaking the power of that speech and the spirit of it reached me. It reached me though spoken in a different tongue. He pleaded with the world and with Germany to avoid the very condition that has developed since. He saw it coming clearly and tried to persuade the world to avoid it, but it seems very difficult for us to avoid the things that we ought to avoid.
I do believe in the collective system. I think that the League of Nations if given the moral support of all the nations could do great things. I believe in an international police force; that I think is necessary. It is the

only sort of army to have at all and it should be sufficiently strong, acting for all the nations, to bring the aggressor into conformity with the ideas of all.
May I give a quotation from a speech delivered by Field Marshal Sir William Robertson in London, England at a chamber of commerce banquet on November 8, 1927. In this speech he said:
Again, we no longer agree, without qualifications, that the best way of preventing war is to prepare for it. Instead of preventing war, we know that preparations are apt to precipitate it.
And again:
War has become, in short, a wholly detestable thing; is almost, if not quite, as disastrous to victor as to vanquished; and consequently many people condemn it as a failure, hate the very word war, and demand all-round measures of disarmament.
While the amount of money we are voting is not large compared to the military budgets of other nations, if the methods it provides for are not adequate in protecting us against the danger that threatens, then even the amount voted here, something approximating $15,000,000, could be spent to very much better purpose in the dominion at the present time.
Has the minister the information regarding the name of the firm that supplied the tobacco to the relief camps?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have not yet been
able to ascertain the name of the firm that supplied the tobacco but I would call the attention of the committee to the result of the investigation I made with regard to the potatoes which the hon. gentleman kindly sent across the chamber-potatoes brought from one of the camps at White Rock. He made some statements with regard to the contract under which these potatoes were supplied. I obtained a copy of the contract and ascertained that tenders were called for from thirteen different firms and people of whom four were individual farmers, and of the rest one was a farmers' exchange and one the Pacific Coast Growers' Cooperative Association. The contract was let to the lowest tenderer, which was F. R. Stewart and Company, and the price for the potatoes was $25 per ton. My hon. friend gave second hand information that F. R. Stewart and Company paid certain farmers of his acquaintance sums ranging from $3.75 to $5 per ton. I am quite ready to believe the hon. member's statement but I think the committee will agree that it is quite impossible to find out what successful contractors paid to the

farmers from whom they bought potatoes. A letter was written at that time by the Pacific Coast Growers' Cooperation Association and I should like to quote one paragraph which touches upon the difficulty of continuity of supply. It reads:
The growers of this association wish me to convey their thanks and appreciation for being given this opportunity of tendering on relief camp contracts as well as for past business.
We regret however that these contracts call for six month period which means this organization being only in its infancy and not having all facilities intact for handling long term contracts, we feel in justice to the government and all concerned it would be much better for us to cooperate with some wholesale house. If this should he a cold winter vegetables will have to be placed in storage in order to take care of your out of town camps, and if we tendered and our contract was accepted it would mean you would have to pay increased prices to take care of storage.
I suggest that if this association takes this view, there is really little likelihood that individual farmers would be in a position to tender direct.
In connection with tobacco furnished in the camps, the hon. member will recall that in giving the component parts of the $1.30 cost per man per day, it was stated that one and one-third ounces of tobacco was issued each week to the men. It was found that when	a certain	kind of	tobacco	wasfurnished to the camp the men would ask for other kinds and the consequence was that instead of	the actual	tobacco	being issued
each week, so many cents were given to the men so that they would have the opportunity of obtaining the kind of tobacco to which they were accustomed.

I am glad the minister has made this	statement,	because	I was	verycareful to	have my	figures correct.	The
minister stated $25 per ton was paid and the superintendent of the camp told me the the price was $24. I think it would be very easy to ascertain that the wholesale price for potatoes in the Fraser valley was $5 per ton. This was for No. 1 grade and in many cases it was impossible to make a sale. In connection with the continuity of supply, I pointed out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) that the former government of British Columbia purchased from the individual farmers when they were looking after these camps. The cost per meal has increased a few cents under the dominion government as compared with the cost per meal under the provincial government which purchased supplies from different farmers. Investigations at that time proved that there was no difficulty in obtaining supplies in that district.

Questions
In connection with tobacco, I inadvertently gave the wrong company. The company referred to should have been the Macdonald company and not the Imperial. The contract was originally for forty cents and was gradually increased to seventy cents per pound.

I have listened with great interest to the speeches of the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) and Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail). I should like to ask the minister if consideration has been given to the request that a suitable patrol station be located on the Pacific coast in case of attack from the orient. I know this request has been made by different chambers of commerce and associated boards of trade pointing out the strategic positions of the different localities.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
A request of this nature has been received from Prince Rupert. Consideration has been given to the matter but so far it has not been decided to divide the stations on the Pacific coast. I do not mean to say that it may not be done in the future.
Progress reported.
